author: william-guthrie
fields.title: The Christian's Great Interest
fields.description: Guthrie’s plain Scottish guide to the question that matters most: how a person may know whether they truly belong to Christ, and, if not, how to close with him now — the marks of faith and the new creature, the law’s preparing work, and honest answers to the fears that keep people back.
fields.attribution: Public domain — William Guthrie, The Christian’s Great Interest (1658). Text from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library.

fields.title: To the Reader
fields.body_html:
CHRISTIAN READER,

WHILE most people, especially in these days, have proclaimed from the housetops, by their eager pursuit of low and base interests, how much they have forgotten to choose that better part which, once chosen, would never be taken from them, I have made an attempt, such as it is, in the following treatise to draw you away from this unprofitable, though painful, pursuit. I do it by setting before you the greatest of all interests, the “Christian’s Great Interest,” for you to think about seriously and pursue constantly. You may find it strange to see anything in print from my pen, as indeed it is a surprise to me. But necessity has made me, this once, go so much against my own inclination, because some people, without my knowledge, have recently published some imperfect notes of a few of my sermons, thrown together in great confusion, and have put in front of them this empty title, which displeases me as much as the publishing of the thing itself: “A clear, attractive, warming Beam,” etc. For this reason I was persuaded to publish this little work. In it I have deliberately used a very homely and plain style, so that I would not be above the reach of the uneducated and ignorant, whose benefit I have mainly, if not only, had in view (though when I have stretched myself to the utmost, I am below the judicious and more understanding anyway). I have also aimed at brevity in everything, as far as I thought it consistent with plainness and clarity, knowing that the people I am addressing have neither much money to spend on books nor much time to spare for reading. If you are a strict critic, I know you may find several things to pick at. Yet be assured that I had no intention of offending you, nor will your approval alone satisfy me. It is your spiritual building up that I aim at, together with the hope of stirring others more skilled and experienced in this excellent subject to deal at greater length with what I have only briefly touched on. I am

Thy servant in the

Work of the Gospel,

WILLIAM GUTHRIE

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
SINCE there are so many people living under the means of grace who claim, without grounds, a special interest in Christ, and in His favour and His salvation, as our Lord states: “Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name, and in thy name have cast out devils, and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you; depart from Me, ye that work iniquity.” “Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us. But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not.”—“Strive to enter in at the strait gate; for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.” And since many who have good grounds for claiming Christ are not settled in confidence of His favour, but remain in the dark without comfort, hesitating about whether godliness is real in them, and saying little to commend religion to others, especially in their times of difficulty, I will say a little about two things of the greatest importance. The first is, How shall a person know whether he has a true and special interest in Christ, and whether he rightly lays claim to God’s favour and salvation? The second is, If a person falls short of assurance in this test, what course should he take to make God’s friendship and salvation sure to himself?

Question 1. How shall a person know whether he has a true and special interest in Christ, and whether he has, or may rightly lay, claim to God’s favour and salvation?

fields.title: An Interest in Christ May Be Known
fields.body_html:
BEFORE we speak directly to the question, we will set down some things first to prepare the way for the answer.

First, a person’s interest in Christ, or his state of grace, may be known, and with more certainty than people suppose. Indeed, it may be known more easily than many imagine. For not only has the Lord commanded people to know this interest in Him, as something that can be attained: “Examine yourselves whether ye be in the faith,” etc. “Give diligence to make your calling and election sure,” etc. But many of the saints have also come to a clear persuasion of their interest in Christ, and in God as their own God. How often they call Him their God and their Portion! And how persuaded Paul is “that nothing can separate him from the love of God!” So the knowledge of a person’s state of grace can be attained.

And this knowledge that may be attained is no fancy or mere imagination, but is most sure. “Doubtless thou art our Father,” says the prophet in the name of the church. This is clear from the following: 1. A knowledge that gives a rational person comfort in very real difficulties can be no fancy, but must be very sure knowledge. And this knowledge does that: “When the people spake of stoning David, he encouraged himself in the Lord his God.” He says, “He will not be afraid of ten thousands that rise against him.” Compare these words with the following: “But thou, O Lord, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.”—“The Lord is my light, and my salvation, whom shall I fear? the Lord is the strength of my life, of whom shall I be afraid? Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident.” 2. A knowledge of a thing that makes a wise merchant sell all he has in order to keep it safe, that makes a person give up children, lands and life, and suffer the seizing of everything joyfully, is sure knowledge. And this knowledge does that. 3. A knowledge on which a person voluntarily and freely risks his soul as he steps into eternity, with these words in his mouth, “This is all my desire,” must be a sure and certain knowledge and no fancy. And this is such a knowledge.

Again, not only may a godly person come to sure knowledge of his state of grace, but it can be attained more easily than many think. For supposing, as will be proved later, that a person can know the gracious work of God’s Spirit in himself, if he will only reason rationally from it, he will be forced to conclude that he has an interest in Christ, unless he denies clear truths of Scripture. I will use only one here, because we are to speak more directly to this later. A godly person may reason like this: Whoever receives Christ is rightly counted a child of God: “But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God.” But I have received Christ in every sense the word can carry there. For I am pleased with God’s plan of salvation through Christ; I agree to its terms; I welcome the offer of Christ in all His offices, as a King to rule over me, a Priest to offer sacrifice and intercede for me, and a Prophet to teach me; I lay out my heart for Him and towards Him, resting on Him as far as I am able. What else can the word receiving mean? So I may say, and conclude plainly and with good warrant, that I am rightly to count myself God’s child according to the Scripture quoted above, which cannot fail.

The Second thing to set down first is that being savingly in covenant with God is a matter of the highest importance: “It is his life.” And yet very few have or seek a saving interest in the covenant, and many foolishly think they have such a thing without any solid grounds: “Few find, or walk, in the narrow way.” This should alarm people into being serious about the matter, since it is of such great consequence to be in Christ, and since only a few may rightly lay claim to Him. And yet many foolishly imagine they have an interest in Him, deceived by a false confidence, as the foolish virgins were.

The Third thing to set down first is that people must resolve to let Scripture decide this matter of their interest in Christ. The Spirit speaking in the Scripture is the Judge of all disputes: “To the law and to the testimony; if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.” He is the Judge of this one too, whether a person is savingly in covenant with God or not. So do not mock God while you appear to be searching into such a thing. If we prove from Scripture, which is the undisputed rule, that you are in a state of grace and have made a saving covenant with God, then resolve to admit as much and rest in it. And if the opposite appears, let that settle the dispute. Otherwise you are only mocking the Lord, and so “your hands shall be made strong”; for “a jot of his word cannot fail.” So seek eye-salve from Christ, to judge things as the word of God shows them to be.

fields.title: Why So Few Know Their Interest in Christ
fields.body_html:
THE Fourth thing to set down first is this. Although a person’s interest in Christ is of such great importance, and the way to come to know it is set out so plainly in the Scriptures, only a few reach a clear knowledge of it. So that this does not discourage anyone from attempting it, I will mention a few reasons why so few come to a clear knowledge of it. This will also prepare the way for what is to be said later.

The first thing that keeps many from knowing their interest in Christ is their ignorance of some particular principles of religion, such as these:

1. That it was free love in God’s heart, and nothing in man, that moved Him to send a Saviour to complete the work of redemption: “God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.” People are always looking for some grounds for that work in themselves. This leads them away from fitting and high views of the first source and origin of God’s covenant favour to His people, which has no reason, cause or motive in us. And so they cannot come to know their interest.

2. They are ignorant of how that love effectively reveals itself to a person’s heart, so that he has grounds to lay claim to it. Ordinarily, it does this: First, it reveals to him his own fallen state, because of sin and corruption defiling the whole person and anything in him that might be called righteousness: “All these things are loss and dung.” Second, it reveals Christ as the full and satisfying treasure above all things: “The man finds a treasure, for which with joy he selleth all,” etc. Third, it settles the heart and causes it to draw near to a living God in the ordinances: “Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts.” It causes the heart to wait on Him, and Him alone: “My soul, wait thou only upon God.” So, having dropped the seed of God into the heart and formed Christ there, the heart is changed and made new in the work: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” And God’s law is so stamped on the heart in that change that the whole yoke of Christ is commended to the person without exception. The law is acknowledged as “good, holy, just, and spiritual.” From all this, from that new principle of life, flow acts of a new life: “faith worketh by love”; and the person becomes “a servant of righteousness unto God.” This appears especially in spiritual worship, for people then “serve God in spirit and truth; and in the newness of the spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter”; and in tenderness in every kind of conduct, for the person then “exerciseth himself how to keep a conscience void of offence towards God” and towards men. This is the way the love of God reveals itself to a person and works on him, so that he has grounds for laying some good claim to it, and may rightly think that the love that sent a Saviour had in view such a person as has found these things worked out in him. Surely ignorance in this keeps many from knowing their interest in Christ. For if a person does not know how God works with someone so that he may rightly lay claim to His love, which was from eternity, he will wander in the dark and not come to know that he has an interest in Him.

3. Many are also ignorant of this: that God alone is the hope of His people. He is called “the Hope of Israel.” Although qualities within us are evidence of it, it is the resting of the heart on Him as a full blessing and satisfying portion that is faith: “The faith and hope must be in God.” And faith is the only proper condition that gives a right to the saving blessings of the covenant: “To him that worketh not, but believeth—faith is counted for righteousness.” Indeed, if anyone takes liberties here and turns grace into licence, there is without doubt a delusion to that extent, since there “is mercy with him upon condition that it conciliate fear to him.” Indeed, hardly anyone who has found the expressions of God’s love mentioned above worked out in him can make the covenant a cloak for sinful liberty without some measure of spiritual conflict. In this respect “he that is born of God doth not sin,” and “he who doth so sin hath not seen God.” I say, God is the hope of His people, and not their own holiness. If they mean honestly and long seriously to be like Him, many failings should not weaken their hope and confidence, for it rests in Him “who changeth not”; “and if any man sin, he hath an advocate.” Now when people put their hope in anything other than the Lord, it is no wonder they are kept in an unsteady condition, rising and falling with the thing they make the grounds of their hope. For they do not give God the glory due to His name, which He will not give to another. “They who know thy name will put their trust in thee.” “My glory will I not give to another; I am the Lord, that is my name.”

4. Many are ignorant of the different ways and degrees in which God works with His people, and this greatly darkens their knowledge of their interest in Him and their reflection on it. This ignorance consists mainly of three things. 1. They are ignorant of the different degrees and ways of that work of the law which ordinarily deals with people, and of the different ways in which the Lord first brings people to Christ. They do not consider that the jailer is not kept in bondage for an hour, Paul is kept in suspense for three days, and Zacchaeus not for one moment. 2. They are ignorant of, or at least do not consider, how different the degrees of sanctification are in the saints: how honourably it appears before people in some, and how sadly it is blemished in others. Some are very blameless and more free from gross outbreaks, adorning their profession greatly, like Job and Zechariah. These are said to be “perfect and upright, fearing God, and eschewing evil; righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.” Others were subject to very gross and sad evils, like Solomon, Asa and others. 3. They are ignorant of the different ways God shows His face and expresses His presence. Some walk much in the light of God’s face and have much felt fellowship with Him, as David did. Others are “all their days kept in bondage through fear of death.” Surely ignorance of the different ways in which God works and deals with His people greatly darkens the knowledge of their interest in Him, while they usually limit the Lord to one way of working, which He does not keep to, as we have shown in the examples above.

The second thing that darkens people about their interest in Christ is that there is one thing or another in which their heart in some respect condemns them for dealing deceitfully and dishonestly with God. It is not to be expected that those whose heart condemns them for holding on to some known sin against the Lord, which they will not let go, and who are not using the means they know God has appointed to deliver them from it, can come to clearness about their interest. Nor can those come to clearness who know of some positive duty commanded them in their position which they deceitfully dodge and avoid, not taking it up cheerfully, or unwilling to be led into it. These too are in some respect condemned by their own heart, as the first kind are. In that case it is difficult to come to a clear knowledge of their state. “If our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence towards God.” It is implied here that a self-condemning heart empties a person’s confidence before God in proportion.

I do not deny that people may on good grounds plead an interest in Christ even when sin is prevailing: “Iniquities prevail against me; as for our transgressions thou shalt purge them away.” “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then, with the mind I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.” But it is hard to reach, if it can be reached at all, when the heart is dealing deceitfully and harbouring known dishonesty in any particular. So let people clear themselves of the particular thing they know only too well. It is the thing that hinders them, spoiling their confidence and access in all their drawing near to God: “Yet ye have forsaken me, and served other gods: wherefore I will deliver you no more.” The Lord throws the people’s idolatries back at them, and their request is rejected because of them. It is the thing that draws the heart away first thing in the morning and last thing at night, like “an oven heated at night, and it burneth as a flaming fire in the morning,” as is said of the wicked. It often takes up their thoughts on their bed, as it is said of some, “He deviseth mischief upon his bed,” etc. It is the thing that ordinarily leads the heart away during religious duty, and the memory of which has more power to enliven and stir the spirits than the memory of God, so that “their heart is after the heart of some detestable thing.” It is the thing that stands in people’s way when they want to take hold of the promise, as God throws people’s sins back at them when they meddle with His covenant: “What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldst take my covenant in thy mouth?” etc. That is the thing that hinders the knowledge of a state of grace. Let it go, and it will be easier to come to know that you have an interest in Christ.

The third thing that hinders many from knowing their interest in Christ is a spirit of laziness and careless neglect. They complain that they do not know whether they are in Christ or not. But just as few take trouble to be in Him, so few take trouble to test whether they are in Him. It is a work and a business that cannot be done asleep: “Examine yourselves whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves: know ye not your own selves?” etc. The several words used there, examine, prove, know, show that there is labour in it: “Diligence must be used to make our calling and election sure.” It is a business beyond flesh and blood. The “holy anointing which teacheth all things” must make us “know the things freely given to us of God.” Shall the Lord give a matter of such great concern, and will it not even be inquired after, that He might do it for people? Be ashamed, you who spend so much time reading romances, adorning your bodies, hawking and hunting, consulting the law about your outward position in the world, and perhaps in worse things than these. Be ashamed, you who spend so little time searching into this: whether you are an heir of glory or not, whether you are on the way that leads to heaven or on the way that will land you in darkness for ever. You who think this beneath you, and unworthy of your trouble for any part or minute of your time, have probably, in God’s reckoning, judged yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, so that you will have no share with God’s people in this matter.

The fourth thing that darkens the knowledge of an interest in Christ is that people do not settle on what would satisfy them. They complain that God will not show them what He is going to do with them, yet they cannot say they know what would satisfy them about His purpose. This is a sad thing. Are we to think those people serious who have never yet settled on what would satisfy them, and are not earnestly inquiring into what should satisfy them? If the Lord had left us in the dark on that matter, we would be less without excuse. But since the grounds of satisfaction and the true marks of an interest in Christ are so clear and so frequent in Scripture, and so “many things written, that our joy may be full,” and “that those who believe may know that they have eternal life,” and since “he that believeth hath the witness of it in himself,” no one can claim an excuse here. We will not go into what may and should satisfy us about our interest here, since we are to speak of it directly later.

The fifth thing that does much to keep people in the dark about their interest in Christ is that they settle on some changeable grounds. These are not so much fitting proofs that an interest in Christ is real as signs of the comfortable state of a triumphant soul sailing before the wind. They are marks which, I grant, are precious in themselves, and which clearly show an interest where they are present. Yet they are such that an interest in Christ may exist without them, and may even be known in good measure. We will touch on a few of them.

First, some think that all who have a true interest in Him are above the prevailing power of every sin. But this is contrary to the words of the Psalmist: “Iniquities prevail against me; as for our transgressions thou shalt purge them away.” There we find that holy man rightly laying claim to pardon while sin is prevailing. It is also contrary to Paul, where he thanks God through Christ as freed from the condemnation of the law, even while a law in his members leads him captive to sin.

Second, some think that all true saints have constant access to God in prayer, and felt answers to prayer at all times. But this is contrary to the many sad experiences of His people, who often complain that they are not heard or regarded by God: “How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? O my God, I cry in the day-time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.”

Third, some think that all who have any true interest in Him have God bearing witness to it, by a high working of that witnessing Spirit of His spoken of here: “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit that we are the children of God.” (More on this later.) And so they keep suspecting their own interest in Christ, because they lack this. But they do not remember that they must first believe and give credit to that “record which God hath given of his Son, that there is life enough in him” for people, and then look for the seal and witness of the Spirit: “In whom, after ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,” etc. As long as people hold fast to these principles and others like them, they can hardly come to know their state of grace, which God has authorised people to prove and make clear to themselves by means other than the things just mentioned.

fields.title: Some Mistakes Concerning an Interest in Christ
fields.body_html:
THE Fifth thing to set down first is the removal of some mistakes that people may easily fall into when they set about proving their interest in Christ.

For example: 1. It is a mistake to think that everyone who is in Christ knows that he is in Him. For many are truly in a state of grace and have a good title to eternal life who do not know it until it is made clear to them later: “These things are written to believers, that they may know they have a true title to eternal life”; that is, that they may know they are believers. So it is implied that they did not know it before.

2. It is a mistake to think that all who come to know their interest in Christ reach an equal certainty about it. One may say, “He is persuaded nothing present, or to come, can separate him from the love of God.” Another gets only this far: “I believe, help my unbelief.”

3. It is a mistake to think that everyone who reaches a strong persuasion of his interest always stays there. For the one who today may say of the Lord, “He is his refuge,” and “his portion,” will at another time say, “He is cut off,” and will ask, “If the truth of God’s promise doth fail for evermore?”

4. It is also a mistake to think that everyone who reaches a good knowledge of their state of grace can formally answer every objection made against it. Yet they may hold fast to the conclusion and say, I “know whom I have believed.” There are few foundations of the Christian religion about which many people are so persuaded that they can formally defend them against every argument brought against them. And yet they may and will hold to the conclusion steadily and rightly. So it is in the case in hand.

5. It is no less a mistake to imagine that the empty, groundless confidence that many profane, ignorant atheists hold is the knowledge of an interest in Christ that we are pleading for. Many falsely claim Him “to be their Father,” and many look for heaven who will be disappointed with the “foolish virgins.” Yet we must not think because of this that all knowledge of an interest is a delusion and a fancy, even though these fools are deceived. For while thousands are deluded, some can say on good and solid grounds, “We know that we are of God, and that the whole world lieth in wickedness.”

fields.title: Drawn to Christ Without a Sensible Work of the Law
fields.body_html:
HAVING set down these things, we must now give some marks by which a person may know whether he is savingly in covenant with God and has a special interest in Christ, so that he may with good warrant lay claim to God’s favour and salvation. We will settle on only two great and principal marks, not wanting to trouble people with many.

But before we begin on these, we will speak of a preparatory work of the law, which the Lord generally uses to prepare His own way in people’s souls. With some people this may carry weight of its own as a mark. It is called the Work of the Law, or the Work of Humiliation. It has some relation to that “spirit of bondage,” corresponds to it now under the New Testament, and usually leads on to the “Spirit of adoption.”

Only let these things be remembered here. 1. We are not to speak of this preparatory work of the law as a negative mark of a true interest in Christ, as if no one might lay claim to God’s favour who has not had this preparatory work in the several steps we are going to describe. For, as we will see, the Lord does not always deal with people that way. 2. The main reason we speak of it is that the Lord deals by some such preparatory work with many whom He effectually calls. To those who have been dealt with like this, it may prove strengthening, and will confirm them in putting more weight on the marks that follow. 3. It may help to encourage others who are under such bondage of spirit, as a good sign that a gracious work will follow. For, as we will explain it, it will rarely be found to go wrong and fail of a gracious outcome. 4. Where God uses such a preparatory work, He does not keep to one way or measure in it, as we will see.

To deal with this preparatory work more clearly, we will briefly point out the most ordinary ways by which the Lord savingly leads people into the covenant and draws them to Christ.

I. There are some called from the womb, as John the Baptist was, or in their very early years, before they can be deeply and actively involved in Satan’s ways, as Timothy was. It cannot be supposed that these have such a preparatory work as we are to speak of. And because some people may claim this way of effectual calling, we offer these marks of it, by which those who have been called like this may be confirmed.

1. Such people are usually kept from childhood free from the ordinary pollutions with which children are commonly defiled, such as swearing, lying, mocking religion and religious people, and so on. Those whom God calls effectually, He sanctifies from the time of that effectual calling: “Sin cannot have dominion over them” as over others, “because they are under grace.”

2. Religion is, as it were, natural to them. I mean that they do not need to be pushed hard to religious duties, even when they are only children. They run that way willingly, because there is an inward principle of “love constraining them,” so that they “yield themselves, servants of righteousness,” without outward restraint.

3. Although such people do not know when they first became acquainted with God, yet afterwards such spiritual experiences come on them as the saints in Scripture speak of, whose first conversion we do not hear about. Now and then, on some occasion, they are shut out from God, and then admitted to come nearer again, as they perceive it. Their heart is also further opened by the ordinances, as is said of Lydia. And generally they remember when some particular matter of religion and duty, or some sin they had not noticed before, was revealed to them. Those who can apply these things to themselves have much to say for their effectual calling from their youth.

II. Some are brought to Christ in a sovereign gospel way, when the Lord, by a few words of love that swallow up any work of the law, quickly takes a person prisoner from the very first, as He did Zacchaeus and others who left everything and followed Him at a word spoken by Christ. We hear nothing of a work of the law dealing with them before they come to Christ Jesus.

And because some may claim this way of calling, we will touch on some of the most remarkable things in that dealing with Zacchaeus, to clear and confirm them. 1. He had some desire to see Christ, and such a desire that it made him set aside what some would have thought prudence and discretion, as he climbed a tree to see Him. 2. Christ spoke to his heart, and that word took such hold on him that he at once accepted Christ’s offer with joy and took Christ as Lord, while few people of any standing were following Him. 3. As a result his heart opened to the poor, although it seems he had been a covetous man before. 4. He had a proper sense of his former ways, showing his regard for Moses’ law, and he made this known before the whole company present, not minding putting himself to shame in matters that were probably well known to everyone. 5. On all this, Christ confirms and ratifies the bargain by His word, commending to him the oneness of interest that must exist between him and the saints, and the thought of his own lost condition if Christ had not come and sought him and found him.

We grant that the Lord calls some like this. If anyone can lay claim to the particular things we have just pointed out, they have good confirmation from Scripture of God’s dealing with them. Nor should they trouble themselves over the lack of a distinct preparatory work of the law, if their heart has yielded to Christ, for a work of the law is desirable only for this purpose. That is why Christ offers Himself directly in the Scripture and people are invited to come to Him. And although many will not come to Him who is the guarantor until the spirit of bondage distresses them for their debt, yet if any, on knowing their lost state, would flee and yield to Christ, no one could rightly press a work of the law on them.

As for others whom Christ persuaded by a word to follow Him, whatever He did or however He spoke to them at His first meeting with them, we must reasonably suppose that He then showed them so much of their own need and of His own fullness and excellence that it made them leave everything and run after Him. And if He does that to anyone, we ask for no more, since there is room enough there for the Physician.

So from all this, just as some with whom God has dealt like this may be confirmed and strengthened, there is no ground or occasion for deluded souls to flatter themselves in their condition, who remain ignorant and insensible of their own miseries and of Christ’s all-sufficiency, and hold fast to deceit.

III. There are some brought to Christ in a way that shows His free grace even more plainly. This is when He effectually calls people at the hour of death. We find something of this way recorded in that striking example of the “thief on the cross.” Although this does not seem very relevant to the purpose in hand, we will say a little about it, so that on the one hand people may be slow to judge and pass sentence on themselves or others before their last breath. And we will describe it in such detail that, on the other hand, no one may dare to put off such a great business to the last hour of their life.

We find these things remarkable in that dealing between Christ and the thief. 1. The man falls out with his former companion. 2. He dares not say a wrong word about God, whose hand is on him, but justifies Him in everything that has happened to him. 3. He now sees Jesus Christ persecuted by the world without cause and most unjustly. 4. He recognises Christ as a Lord and a King while His enemies seem to have Him beaten. 5. He believes in a state of glory after death so truly that he prefers a share in it to the present safety of his bodily life, which he knew Christ was able to grant him at that time, so that he might have chosen that with the other thief. 6. Although he was very humbled in himself, so that he pleaded only that Christ would remember him, yet he was nobly daring in throwing himself on the covenant for life and death. And he had so much faith in Christ’s all-sufficiency that he judged that a simple remembering by Christ would satisfactorily settle his business. 7. He rested sweetly in the word Christ spoke to him as the ground of his comfort. All these things are very clear in the case of that poor dying man, and prove a very real work of God on his heart.

While this example may encourage some who cannot yet clearly lay claim to any gracious work of His Spirit to wait for good from God, we earnestly beg everyone, as they love their souls, not to put off the salvation of their souls, hoping for such help from Christ at the end, as too many do. For this was a rare miracle of mercy, by the glory of which Christ triumphed honourably over the disgrace of His cross, and we will hardly find a parallel to it anywhere else in Scripture. Indeed, just as only a few are saved at all (“Many be called, but few chosen”), and fewest of all are saved this way, so the Lord has firmly threatened to laugh at the calamity and not to hear the cry of those who formerly mocked His rebuke and would not listen when He called them: “Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; but ye have set at nought all my counsel and would none of my reproof: I also will laugh at your calamity, I will mock when your fear cometh.” Although this Scripture does not shut the door of mercy on anyone who at the hour of death sincerely judges himself and flees to Christ, as this penitent thief did, yet it certainly implies that very few who reject the offer until then are honoured with repentance as he was. And so their cry, not being sincere and of the right kind, will not be heard.

fields.title: The Work of the Law
fields.body_html:
IV. The fourth and most ordinary way by which many are brought to Christ is by a clear and noticeable work of the law and of humiliation, which we generally call “the spirit of bondage,” as was mentioned before. We do not mean that everyone whose conscience is awakened by sin and fear of wrath really comes to Christ. The opposite appears in Cain, Saul, Judas and others. But there is a conviction of sin, an awakening of conscience and a work of humiliation which, as we will describe it in detail, rarely goes wrong or fails of a gracious outcome, but ordinarily ends in the “Spirit of adoption” and a gracious work of God’s Spirit. And because the Lord deals with many sinners this way, and we find that many are very puzzled about how to judge this work of the law, we will speak of it in detail.

This work is either carried through more violently and suddenly, or it is drawn out more quietly and gently over a longer time, so that its steps are very noticeable. It is more violent in some, as in the jailer, Paul and some other converts in the Acts of the Apostles, on whom Christ broke in in an instant, fell on them as if with fire and sword, and led them captive in a terrifying way. And because some great awakenings under the law are deceptive and come to nothing, if not worse, we will point to some remarkable things in these converts just mentioned which prove that the work of the law on them had a gracious outcome and result. 1. Some word of truth, or some providence, brings the person to a dreadful standstill, with a great stir in the soul. “Some are pricked in heart”; “some fall on trembling.” And this stir is such that the person is brought to his wits’ end: “What wilt thou have me to do?” says Paul; “What must I do to be saved?” says the jailer. 2. The person is content to have salvation and God’s friendship on any terms, as the question implies: “What shall I do?” It is as if he were saying, What would I not do? What would I not give up? What would I not go through? 3. The person accepts the condition offered by Christ and His servants, as is clear in the Scriptures quoted. 4. The person at once comes to share one interest with the saints, joining himself to that persecuted company, showing respect to those he had formerly persecuted, and joining and staying with them in the profession of Christ at all risks. Those whom the Lord has dealt with like this have much to say for a gracious work of God’s Spirit in them. Probably many of them can date their work from a particular time and word or providence, and can give some account of what passed between God and them, and of a noticeable change in them from that time on, just as Paul afterwards gives a good account of God’s work and way with him.

Again, the Lord sometimes carries on this work more calmly, gently and easily, drawing it out so that the several steps of people’s experience under it are very noticeable. It would take us a long time to enlarge on every step of it, so we will touch on the most noticeable things in it.

1. The Lord lays siege to people who have perhaps often refused to yield to Him when He offered Himself in His ordinances. By some word preached, read or pressed on the mind, or by some providence that brings the word home, He attacks the house that is kept in peace by the strong man, the devil. So Christ, who is the stronger man, comes upon him, and by the Spirit of truth fastens on the person the word in which God’s curse is pronounced against such and such sins, which the person knows he is guilty of. The Spirit convinces the person and binds it on him that he is the very person against whom the word of God speaks, because he is guilty of such sins. From some sins the person is led on to see more, until usually he comes to see the sins of his youth, his sins of omission and so on. Indeed, he is led on until he sees himself guilty of breaking almost the whole law. He sees “innumerable evils compassing him,” as David says in a time of trial. A person in this situation will sometimes see dreadful sights of sin, and is quick to see a link to almost every sin. This is how “the Spirit cometh and convinceth of sin.”

2. The Lord shakes a particular stronghold in the garrison, a refuge of lies, to which the person runs when his sins are uncovered to him like this. The poor person claims faith in Christ, by which he thinks his burden is taken off him, as the Pharisees said, “We have one Father, even God”; they claim a special relationship to God as a common Lord. The Spirit of God drives the person out of this by the truth of the Scriptures, proving that he has no true faith, and so no interest in Christ or any true saving grace. He shows clearly the difference between true grace and the counterfeit fancies the person has in him, and between him and the truly godly, as Christ labours to do with the Jews: “If God were your Father, ye would love me. Ye are of the devil, for ye do the lusts of such a father.” So “fear surpriseth the hypocrite in heart,” especially when the Lord shows him conditions, not easily met, in many of the promises he trusted most. He now sees that grace and faith are something different from what he once thought them to be. In some respect we may apply this word here: “The Spirit convinceth him of sin, because he hath not believed on the Son.” He is particularly convinced of unbelief. He now sees a vast distance between himself and the godly, who he thought before only outstripped him in some unnecessary, proud, hateful strictness. He now sees that he has been deluded and is on the broad way with the perishing crowd. And so, seeing his misery, he lies down under his own burden, which until now he thought Christ was carrying for him. He now begins to shy away from the promises, because of that and other words like it: “What hast thou to do to take my covenant in thy mouth?” etc.

3. The person becomes anxious about his salvation and begins to take it to heart as the one thing needful. He is brought with the jailer to this: “What shall I do to be saved?” His salvation becomes the main thing for him. It was the least of his thoughts before, but now it takes over, and he pays little regard to other things. Since his soul is ready to perish, “what shall it profit him to gain the world, if he lose his soul?” Some here are very troubled by thoughts of an unchangeable decree against them, and by fears of a sudden death that may strike them before they get matters settled. Some are tormented with fears that they are guilty of the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is unpardonable, and so are driven to a dangerous extreme, with Satan constantly throwing at them many sad examples of people who have miserably put an end to their own lives. But they are in the hand of One who “knoweth how to succour them that are tempted.”

4. When a person is in danger of being lost like this, the Lord works a mercy that comes before him, quietly and secretly holding him up. He does this by pressing on his mind that his salvation is possible, leading the person to remember many proofs of God’s free and rich grace in pardoning gross offenders such as Manasseh, who was a bloodthirsty idolater and had dealings with the devil, and yet obtained mercy. He also brings to mind other Scriptures that offer grace and favour to all alike who will yield to Christ, whatever they have been before. So the person is brought again to this: “What shall I do to be saved?” This implies that he sees it is possible to be saved, otherwise he would not ask the question. He applies that word, or one like it, to himself: “It may be ye shall be hid in the day of the Lord’s anger.” He now finds nothing shutting him out from mercy, if he has a heart for it. Although perhaps at this point the person does not see that it is the Lord who is holding him up, afterwards he can say that “when his foot was slipping, God’s mercy held him up,” as the Psalmist says in another case. And he will say afterwards that when he “was as a beast, and a fool, in many respects, God held him by the hand.”

5. After this discovery that it is possible to be saved, a desire is stirred up in the soul. This is obvious from that same expression, “What shall I do to be saved?” But sometimes this desire is misdirected, when it comes out like this: “What shall I do that I may work the works of God?” In that case the person, who was formerly perplexed with fear and anxiety about his salvation, wants to do some work of his own to get himself out. Here he suddenly resolves to do everything that is commanded and to give up every evil way (yet greatly mistaking Christ Jesus), and so begins to take some courage again, “establishing his own righteousness; but not submitting unto the righteousness of God.” At this the Lord makes a new attack on him, to show him his utterly fallen state in himself, so that room may be made for the guarantor, as Joshua did with the people when he found them so bold in their promises: “Ye cannot serve the Lord,” he says, “for he is a holy God, a jealous God,” etc. In this new attack the Lord: 1. Sets the spirituality of the law against the person. The commandment comes with a new charge in its spiritual meaning. “The law came,” says Paul, that is, in its spiritual meaning; Paul had never seen such a view of the law before. 2. God, in perfect holiness, loosens the restraining bonds He had put on the person’s corruption, and lets it not only work and swell within him, but threaten to break out in all his outward members. So sin grows bold and kicks against the law, becoming exceedingly sinful: “But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead. For I was alive without the law once; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. Was then that which is good made death unto me! God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful.” 3. The Lord shows the person, more now than ever before, the uncleanness of his righteousness and the stains in his best things. These things kill the person, and he dies to his own self-righteousness and despairs of relief in himself, unless it comes from somewhere else.

6. After many ups and downs here, the person generally decides to withdraw. He wants to be alone; he cannot keep company as before. Like people in a besieged city who, when they see they cannot hold out and would be glad of any good terms from the besieging enemy, go into council to decide on something, so the person here withdraws so that he may talk with himself. This is like “communing with our own heart.” In this way God leads into the wilderness so that He may speak to the heart. When the person has withdrawn, the thoughts of his heart, which were scattered in the earlier steps of his experience, crowd in here more noticeably. We will put them in this order. 1. The person thinks of his unhappy folly in taking up arms against God. Here there are many thoughts of former ways, with a blushing face and self-loathing: “Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall loathe yourselves in your own sight,” etc. It is like the Psalmist: “His sin is ever before him.” 2. Then he remembers how many good opportunities of yielding to God he has shamefully lost. His spirit is ready to faint when he remembers it, as is said in another case: “When I remember these things I pour out my soul in me.—O my God, my soul is cast down within me.—Deep calleth unto deep: all thy waves are gone over me.” 3. He now thinks of many Christians whom he mocked and despised in his heart, and persuades himself now that they are happy, having chosen the better part. He thinks of the condition of those who wait on Christ as the Queen of Sheba did of Solomon’s servants: “Happy are thy servants,” she says, “who stand continually before thee, and that hear thy wisdom.” “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house,” etc. He wishes he could be one of the lowest who have any relationship to God. As the prodigal son says, he would be “one of his Father’s hired servants.” 4. Then he calls to mind the good report that has gone out about God, according to the testimony of the prophet, who knew that God was a gracious “God and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness,” etc. The free and generous promises and offers of grace come in here, and the glorious dealings that have happened to sinners of every kind, according to Scripture’s account of God. 5. He thinks to himself, Why has God spared me so long? And why have I been given such a sight of my sin? And why has He kept me from destroying myself with my own hand by choosing some unhappy way out? Why has He made this strange change in me? Perhaps it is in His heart to do me good. Oh, may it be so! Although not all these thoughts are present in everyone’s preparatory work, they are present with many, and are very promising where they are.

7. After all these thoughts and meditations, the person resolves more seriously than ever before to pray, and to make some attempt with God, for life or death. He concludes, “It can be no worse with him; for if he sit still he perisheth,” as the lepers say. He considers, with the perishing prodigal son, “that there is bread enough in his Father’s house and to spare, whilst he perisheth for want.” So he goes to God, for he does not know what else to make of his condition, as the prodigal son does. And perhaps he decides what he will say. But things easily change when he is set before God, as the prodigal son forgot some of his prepared prayers: “I will arise and go to my father, and, will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against Heaven, and before thee, and am no more worthy to be called thy son; make me as one of thy hired servants. And he arose and came unto his father, and said unto him, Father, I have sinned against Heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.”

And now when he comes before God, more noticeably than ever before: 1. He begins, like the tax collector, afar off, with many thorough confessions and self-condemnations, of which he is very generous: “I have sinned against Heaven, and before thee, and am no more worthy,” etc. 2. Now his thoughts are taken up with whether his prayer will be heard, which he did not usually question much. He now knows what the saints’ expressions about the hearing of their prayers mean. 3. It is noticeable in this approach that there are many broken sentences, like the Psalmist’s, “But thou, O Lord, how long?”, filled out with sighs and “groanings which cannot be uttered,” and with earnest looking upward, which says more than can easily be put into words. 4. There are usually some interruptions and, as it were, digressions. The person speaks sometimes to the enemy, sometimes to his own heart, sometimes to the crowd in the world, as David does in other cases: “O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end.” “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God, for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.” “O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame?” 5. It is noticeable here that sometimes the person will stop and be silent, to hear some faint whisper of a joyful sound glancing across the mind, or some news in a broken word of Scripture, which perhaps the person hardly knows to be Scripture, or whether it has come from God or is a hint from Satan to deceive him. Yet he has resolved only to “hear what God the Lord will speak,” as on another occasion. 6. Clearer promises come into the person’s mind, which he tries to take hold of, but he is beaten off with objections, as the Psalmist is in another case: “But thou art holy—but I am a worm.” Now it is about the dawning of the day with the person, and faith will stir as soon as the Lord gives “the joyful sound.” This is the substance of the covenant, which may be summed up briefly in these words: “Christ Jesus is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him.”

We cannot speak any further of the person’s experience as a preparatory work, for what follows is more than preparatory. Yet so that the experience may appear complete and full, we will add here that after all these things, perhaps after many answers of different kinds, the Lord powerfully conveys the knowledge of His covenant into the heart and settles the heart to accept it. And God now draws the heart to Christ, and lays out the heart for Him, in such a way that the work cannot go wrong. For now the heart is so enlarged for Him that less cannot satisfy and more is not desired, like the Psalmist: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? or whom have I desired on earth beside thee?” The soul now resolves to die if He commands it, yet at His door and facing towards Him.

We have described this preparatory work at some length, not binding anyone to such a work in all these particulars. We only say that the Lord deals like this with some. And where He so convinces of sin, corruption and emptiness of self, makes a person take salvation to heart as the one thing needful, and sets him to work using the means God has appointed for relief, I say, such a work will rarely be found to fail of a good outcome and a gracious result.

fields.title: The Law's Work in the Saved and in Hypocrites
fields.body_html:
Objection. Hypocrites and reprobates have great stirrings of conscience and deep convictions about sin, which sometimes set them to work. I suspect that any preparatory work of the law I ever had was only the same as theirs.

Answer. It is hard to give sure, essential distinctions between the preparatory work in those in whom Christ is afterwards formed and the legal stirrings that are sometimes found in reprobates. If there were not some gracious result of these convictions and awakenings of conscience in the Lord’s people, and other marks we will speak of later, it would be hard to settle on any clear difference in these legal stirrings. Yet in answer to the objection I will offer some things that will rarely be found in the stirrings of reprobates, and that are usually found in the work of the law that has a gracious outcome.

1. The convictions of hypocrites and reprobates are usually confined to a few very gross sins. Saul admits nothing more than “persecuting of David.” Judas admits only “betraying of innocent blood.” But usually the convictions by which the Lord prepares His own way in the soul, although they may begin with one or more gross particular sins, do not stop there. The person is led on to see many breaches of the law, and “innumerable evils compassing him,” as David says on seeing his sin. And at the same time, that universal conviction, if I may call it that, is not general, like the way we usually hear insensible people say “that in all things they sin.” It is particular and detailed, as Paul afterwards spoke of himself. He is not only the “chief of sinners,” but specifically he was a “blasphemer, a persecutor.”

2. The convictions that hypocrites have seldom reach their corruption, that body of death which produces a dislike of what is good and strongly inclines to what is evil. Generally, where we find hypocrites speaking of themselves in Scripture, they speak loftily and with some conceit about their freedom from corruption. The Pharisees say to the poor man, “Thou wast altogether born in sin, and dost thou teach us?”, as if they themselves were not as corrupt by nature as he was. They speak this way about great sins, as Hazael did: “Am I a dog, that I should do this great thing?” They speak this way in taking on duty too, as that scribe said: “Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.” See how the people speak: “Then they said to Jeremiah, The Lord be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not even according to all things for the which the Lord thy God shall send thee to us. Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the Lord our God, to whom we send thee; that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the Lord our God.” They undertake to do everything God commands them, so that in any case they are still “going about to establish their own righteousness, not submitting unto the righteousness of God.” But I may say that convictions and struggles about corruption, and that body of death which inclines them to evil and disables them for good, are not the least part of the work where the Lord is preparing His own way. Such people usually judge themselves very wretched because of a body of sin, and are at their wits’ end how to be delivered, as Paul says when he is struggling with it afterwards: “O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”

3. It will generally be found that the convictions in hypocrites are either not so serious that some other business will not put them out of mind before any satisfaction is found. So it was with Cain, who went and built a city, and we hear no more of his convictions. Felix went away until a more convenient time, and we hear no more of his trembling. Or, if that work does become very serious, it runs to the other extreme, despair of relief, leaving no room for escape. So we find Judas very serious in his convictions, yet he grew desperate and hanged himself. But where the Lord prepares His own way, the work is both so serious that the person cannot be put off it until he finds some satisfaction, and yet under that very seriousness he lies open to relief. Both are clear from the jailer’s words, “What must I do to be saved?” This serious inquiry after relief is a very noticeable thing in the preparatory work that leads on to Christ. Yet we want no one to put too much weight on these things, since God has provided clear differences between the precious and the vile.

Objection. I still fear that I have not had as thorough a sight of my sin and misery as the Lord gives to many whom He effectually calls, especially to great sinners such as I am.

Answer. It is true that the Lord gives some people strong impressions of their sin and misery, and they are put under great legal terrors by them. But just as not everyone is brought in by that noticeable preparatory work of the law, as we showed before, so even those who are dealt with in that way go through it very differently, both in the degree of terror and in how long the work lasts. The jailer had a violent work that lasted a very short time. Paul had a work that lasted three days. Some people are “in bondage, through fear of death, all their days.” So we must not limit the Lord to one way of working here. The main thing we are to look at in these legal awakenings and convictions of sin and misery is whether the Lord achieves in us the purposes for which these stirrings and convictions are usually sent into the soul. If those purposes are achieved, it is well, and we are not to trouble ourselves any further about a preparatory work. Now the purposes God seeks to accomplish with sinners by these legal terrors and awakenings of conscience are four.

First, the Lord shows people their sin and misery to drive them out of themselves and to put them out of love with their own righteousness. People naturally have high thoughts of themselves and lean strongly towards the covenant of works. So the Lord shows them so much of their sin and corruption, even in their best things, that they are made to loathe themselves and despair of relief in themselves. And so they are forced to flee out of themselves and away from the covenant of works, to seek refuge elsewhere: “They become dead to themselves and the law,” as far as justification is concerned. Then “have they no more confidence in the flesh.” This is assumed in the offers of Christ, “coming to seek and save that which is lost,” and “to be a physician to those who are sick.”

The second great purpose is to commend Christ Jesus to people’s hearts above all things, so that they may fall in love with Him and turn to that treasure and jewel which alone makes rich. In doing so they may serve the Lord’s design in planning the gospel, which was to display His free grace through Christ Jesus in the salvation of people. Seeing his own misery and perishing condition by nature is a quick way to make a person value Christ highly, who alone can set such a wretch free. Indeed, it leads a person to a high regard not only for Christ but also for everything connected with that way of salvation, such as grace, the new covenant, faith and so on. And it makes him carefully gather and store up his Michtams, or golden Scriptures, to confirm his interest in these things.

The third great purpose is to deter and frighten people away from sin, to make them quarrel with it, and to make them consent to put their neck under His whole yoke. God kindles some sparks of hell in people’s breasts by showing them their sin, as a ready means of making them stand in awe from then on, knowing “how bitter a thing it is to depart from the Lord.” So we find rest offered to the weary on condition that they take Christ’s yoke on them: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart; and ye shall find rest unto your souls.” And God offers to own people as their God and Father on condition that they allow Belial no peaceful home: “What fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? and what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing, and I will receive you, and will be a father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.”

The fourth great purpose is to bring people to a patient and thankful submission to all the Master’s pleasure. This is a remarkable work: “Then shalt thou remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more, because of thy shame, when I am pacified towards thee, for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord.” The sight of his own vileness and what he deserves makes a person silent, and makes him lay his hand on his mouth, whatever God does to him: “I was dumb, and opened not my mouth, because thou didst it.” “God hath punished us less than our iniquities.” “I will bear the indignation of the Lord, because I have sinned.” The person does not care what God does to him or how He deals with him, as long as He saves him from the wrath to come that he deserves. Also, any mercy is a great mercy to someone who has seen such a view of himself. He is “less than the least of mercies”; “any crumb falling from the Master’s table is welcome”; he thinks it rich “mercy that he is not consumed.” This is what wonderfully makes God’s poor afflicted people so silent under their lot and satisfied with it. Indeed, they think that anyone whose transgressions God has pardoned deserves hell if he opens his mouth at anything God does to him.

So then, to satisfy the objection, I say this: if the Lord has driven you out of yourself, commended Christ to your heart above all things, and made you resolve in His strength to wage war against every known sin, and you are in some measure like a weaned child, resting in what He does to you and wanting to lay your hand on your mouth thankfully, then your convictions of sin and misery, and whatever you plead as a preparatory work, are enough, and you are to argue no more about it. Only take this advice: seek every day fresh discoveries and a fresh sense of your lost condition because of your old and new sins; seek fresh help in Christ, who is a priest for ever to make intercession; and have the work of sanctification and of patience with thankfulness often renewed and stirred up. For something of that work which humbles you, exalts Christ and conforms you to His will must go with you throughout your whole life in this world.

fields.title: Of Faith
fields.body_html:
WE come now to speak of some clearer and surer marks by which people may discover their state of grace and their interest in Christ. The first thing by which people may know it is their accepting Christ in the gospel, in which He is held out. This is believing, or faith, which is the condition of the covenant: “It is of faith, that it might be by grace.” “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved.” Now although, strictly speaking, it is hard to prove an interest by faith, since faith is our very interest in Him, yet the heart’s accepting of Christ Jesus is so noticeable in itself that we may well put it among the marks of a state of grace. And if a person can show that he believes on and in Christ Jesus, he proves by this a very real interest in Him.

Many shy away from this as a mark on one of these three grounds:

1. Some think faith is a difficult, mysterious thing, hard to attain. To them I say, Do not be mistaken; faith is not as difficult as many think it is. I grant that true faith, in even the smallest degree, is the gift of God and beyond the power of flesh and blood, for God must draw people to Christ: “No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him.” “Unto you it is given, in the behalf of Christ, to believe on him.” Yet it would be a slur on Christ and on all He has done to say it is a matter of insurmountable difficulty, as is clear: “The righteousness which is of faith, speaketh on this wise, Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down from above; or, Who shall descend into the deep? that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead. But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart; that is, the word of faith which we preach. That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart, that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved: for with the heart man believeth unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For the Scripture saith, Whosoever believeth on him, shall not be ashamed.” According to that Scripture, it would amount to saying that Christ did not come from heaven, has not risen from the dead and has not ascended victorious to heaven. I say, He has made the way to heaven very easy, and faith, the condition required on our part, easier than people imagine. To understand this better, consider that justifying faith is not believing that I am elected, or that God loves me, or that Christ died for me, or the like. These things are indeed very difficult, and almost impossible at first for serious people to reach, while natural atheists and deluded hypocrites find no difficulty in asserting all of them. I say, true justifying faith is none of these things. Nor is it simply believing any sentence that is written or that can be thought of. I grant that the one who believes on Christ Jesus believes what God has said about man’s sinful, miserable condition by nature, and believes it to be true that “there is life in the Son, who was slain, and is risen again from the dead,” and so on. But none of these, nor believing many such truths, amounts to justifying faith, or to that believing on the Son of God spoken of in Scripture. For then it would be simply an act of the understanding. But true justifying faith, which we are now looking for as a good mark of an interest in Christ, is chiefly and principally an act or work of the heart and will, presupposing several things about the truth in the understanding: “With the heart it is believed unto righteousness” (Rom. 10:10). And although it seems in verse 9 of that chapter that a person is saved on condition that he believes this truth, “God raised Christ from the dead,” yet we must understand something more there and in verse 10 than believing the truth of that statement. For besides the fact that all devils have that faith by which they believe that God raised Christ from the dead, the Scripture has clearly explained justifying faith as a receiving of Christ: “As many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” The receiving of Christ is explained there as believing on his name. It is also called a staying on the Lord, a trusting in God, often mentioned in the Psalms, and the word means a leaning on him. It is a believing on Christ: “This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent”; and it is often expressed that way in the New Testament. When God makes people believe savingly, He is said to draw them to Christ. And when the Lord invites them to believe, He calls them to come to Him: “All that the Father giveth me, shall come to me; and him that cometh to me, I will in nowise cast out. No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” The kingdom of heaven is like a man finding a jewel and falling in love with it: “The kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof, goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant-man seeking goodly pearls; who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.” Now, I say, this acting of the heart on Christ Jesus is not as difficult a thing as people think. Should something that consists largely in desire be thought a mysterious and difficult thing? If people have only an appetite, they have it, for they are “blessed that hunger after righteousness.” If you are willing, you are welcome. Is it such a complicated matter, of insurmountable difficulty, earnestly to look to that exalted Saviour? “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth.” Or to receive something that is offered, held out and declared to be mine, if I will only accept it and take it, and in a sense “open my mouth” and let it in? “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” Faith is such a thing as this, if not less. Oh, if only I could persuade people what justifying faith is, which makes Christ my own! We often frighten people away from their rightful rest and peace by making them think faith is some deep, mysterious thing, and by raising unnecessary doubts about it, which needlessly darken it.

2. Some make no use of this mark, because they think it a high and presumptuous crime to claim something as excellent as the very condition of the new covenant. To them I say, You need not be so startled at it, as if it were great pride to claim it. For whatever true faith is, people must resolve to have it, or nothing at all. All other marks are useless without it; a thousand other things will not do the job. “Unless a man believe, he abideth in the state of condemnation.” “He that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. He that believeth not the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abideth on him.”

3. Others do not touch this noble mark of faith because they think it a very difficult task to find faith where it is. To them I say, It is not so difficult to find it, since “he that believeth hath the witness in himself.” It is something that can be known by serious searching. We may do much to find it out by the preparatory work that comes before it in many people: grasping and believing one’s own lost state, and that one cannot work out one’s own salvation, and that there is satisfying fullness in Christ, very desirable if one could reach it, together with serious attention to this, with a heart laid open for relief. We may also find it by its ordinary companions, such as liking Christ’s rule, His kingly and prophetic office, and a desire to give oneself up wholly to Him to be at His disposal. And we may find it by its natural consequences, such as being acquitted by the word, my own conscience acquitting me according to the word, a heart-purifying work, a working by love and so on. I say, not only may we know faith by these things, but it can be recognised by itself and by its own nature. I do not deny that there must be some help from God’s Spirit, “by which we know what is freely given unto us of God,” and also that God has provided many evidences and marks as precious helps by which people may make faith clearer to themselves: “These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God, that ye may know that ye have eternal life.” Yet I still say that faith, or believing, which is some acting of the heart on Christ in the gospel and dealing with Him there, can be recognised of itself and by itself by a judicious, understanding person with an ordinary influence of the Spirit, unless the Lord, for reasons known to Himself, clouds over a person’s power of reflection, by which he should grasp and perceive what is in him.

This justifying faith, which we say can be recognised so clearly, is expressed in Scripture in various ways, in the Lord’s deep wisdom and gracious condescension, according to the different ways it acts on God and goes out after Him, so that everyone who has it may find and recognise it in his own mould. Sometimes it acts by a desire for union with Him in Christ. This is the looking to Him in Isaiah: “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth.” This seems to be a weak act of faith, and far below other acts of it at other times, perhaps in the same person. People will look at what they dare not approach, at what they think they dare not touch or embrace. They may look at someone they dare not speak to. Yet God has made the promise to faith acting in this way, as the Scripture just quoted shows. And He has done this mercifully and wisely, for this is sometimes the only noticeable way in which some people’s faith acts. Other such acts or outgoings of faith are expressed in Scripture as “hungering and thirsting after righteousness,” and as willing: “and whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.”

Again, this faith sometimes goes out in the act of reclining, or leaning on the Lord, the soul then taking Christ as a resting stone; and God has held Him out like that, although He is a stumbling stone to others. This acting of faith is hinted at in the expressions trusting in God and staying on God, so often mentioned in Scripture, and precious promises are made to this acting of faith: “God will keep them in perfect peace whose minds are stayed on him; because such do trust in him. Trust in the Lord; for with him is everlasting strength.” “They that trust in the Lord shall be as Mount Zion, which abideth for ever.” I say, the Lord has made promises to this way of faith’s acting, knowing that it will often go out after Him in this way with many people, and that this way of its acting will be the most noticeable to them.

Sometimes it goes out after God by an act of waiting. When the soul has something hanging before God and has not received a satisfying answer about it, then faith waits, and so it has the promise, “They shall not be ashamed that wait for me.” Sometimes it acts in a determined way on the Lord, when the soul sees God thrusting it away and threatening its ruin: “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.” The faith of that poor woman of Canaan, so highly praised by Christ, went out in this way, acting with determination over difficulties. And the Lord says much good of it and to it, because some will sometimes be driven to exercise faith that way, and so they have this for their encouragement. It would be tedious to give examples of all the different ways in which faith acts on Christ, exercises itself about Him and goes out after Him. I may say they match the various conditions of man. Faith, which God has appointed to trade and travel between Christ and man, as the instrument that conveys His fullness to man and maintains union and fellowship with Him, accordingly acts in various and different ways on God in Christ. For faith is the very laying out of a person’s heart according to God’s plan of salvation by Christ Jesus, “in whom it pleased the Father that all fulness should dwell.” So whichever way Christ turns, faith turns and points that way. Now He turns every way in which He can be useful to poor man, and so faith acts on Him accordingly, to draw out of that fullness according to a person’s case and condition. For example, the soul is naked, without a covering to keep it from the storm of God’s wrath; Christ is fine clothing. So faith’s work here is to “put on the Lord Jesus.” The soul is hungry and thirsty for something that may satisfy it for ever; Christ Jesus is “milk, wine, water, the bread of life, and the true manna.” He is “the feast of fat things, and of wine refined.” So the work and exercise of faith is to “go, buy, eat and drink abundantly.” The soul is pursued by guilt to a greater or lesser degree and cannot answer the charge; Christ Jesus is the city of refuge and the high priest there, and during His priesthood, which is for ever, the poor person who gets there is safe. So the work and exercise of faith is “to flee thither for refuge, to lay hold on the hope set before us.” In a word, in whatever way He may benefit poor man, He declares Himself able to do it. And in whatever way He holds Himself out in the Scriptures, faith points towards Him that way. If He is a Bridegroom, faith will go out in a marriage relationship. If He is a Father, faith pleads that the person is a child. If He is a Shepherd, faith pleads that the person may be one of His sheep. If He is a Lord, faith calls Him that, which no one can do except by the Spirit of Jesus. If He died and rose again for our justification, faith “believeth God hath raised him” on that account. Wherever He is, faith wants to be there; and whatever He is, faith wants to be something like Him. For by faith the heart is laid out in breadth and length for Him. Indeed, when the fame and report of Him goes out in His truth, although faith does not see much, it still “believeth on his name,” on the very report He has sent out about Himself.

But to avoid mistakes here, consider these things. 1. Although justifying faith acts in so many ways, not every believer who has a good title to Christ Jesus has all these different workings and exercises of faith. His condition does not require them. And the Master is also pleased at times, for reasons known to Himself, not to lead out the faith of some people in all these ways, even when their need (as they see it) calls for such workings of faith. Surely not everyone dares to say, “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.” Many would not have kept on with the woman of Canaan I spoke of, but would have been discouraged and given up the pursuit. This is why Christ praises the faith of some highly above the faith of others, such as the centurion and the woman of Canaan. Many good people are very troubled about their faith because it does not go out in all the ways we find recorded in Scripture. But hardly anyone will be found whose faith has worked in all these ways.

2. Many of these workings of faith grow stronger and weaker. Sometimes they are strong, vigorous and noticeable, and sometimes they fail and unbelief prevails. So it would be an uncertain thing to judge a person’s state by them. We find the saints sometimes very unlike themselves in the workings of their faith, as we showed before.

3. Each one of these workings of faith speaks well of the person in whom it is found, and has promises attached to it, as we have said.

4. Although these workings of faith have promises attached to them, that does not make them the condition of the new covenant. For then everyone would need to have each one of them, which is not true, as we said before.
