A promise is made to the one who overcomes, but perseverance is not the condition of the new covenant, though the covenant does assume it. There are promises in Scripture made to the exercise of every grace, but only faith is the condition of the covenant. So I say these promises are made to these workings of faith, not as such, but because they presuppose justifying faith, which is the condition of the covenant. All these are workings of faith, but not of faith as it justifies. Therefore:

5. There is something common to all gracious people, which all the workings of faith mentioned above may be taken to presuppose, and in which the nature and essence of justifying faith consists. It is the heart’s satisfaction with God’s plan of salvation by Christ: when a person is pleased with God’s way of satisfying justice through Christ Jesus, in whom all fullness now dwells by the Father’s pleasure. When the soul and heart rest in that, then they believe to salvation. Just as at first the Lord made man suited to the covenant of works by creating him perfect, and so making him able to carry out His will in that covenant, so under the new covenant, when God gives man the new heart, He puts the idea and stamp of His whole plan in the new covenant on the person, so that there is harmony there with God’s will. So he bears the image of the second Adam, Christ Jesus. This is a large part of the new heart, and is most opposed to works, since the person now completely falls away from works, “becoming dead to the law” as regards justification, “by the body of Christ.” When a person sees that God has devised a way of satisfying divine justice and recovering lost man by the incarnation of Christ, he thinks this such a good and sure way that he completely gives up on the law, as I said before, and takes hold of this plan. This is believing, or faith, very opposite to works and to all resting on them. It cannot fail to be present in all gracious people, even in those in whom many of the workings of faith are not to be found. It clearly presupposes that a person knows his distress, with no relief at all in himself. It presupposes known fullness in Christ as the only sufficient relief. It implies a kind of making one’s own, for the heart, being pleased with that plan, inclines towards it to that extent. This is clearly presupposed in all the workings of faith spoken of before. The one who hungers greedily has this; the one who leans has this; the one who puts on Christ has this, and so on. This is to count “Christ the wisdom and power of God” to salvation, which is what He is said to be to all who believe. They count that plan wise and sure and worthy of God, and that is believing. For this reason “Christ, who is the rejected stone to many, is precious to them who believe,” a fitting stone to restore, strengthen and beautify the tottering building and structure of lost man. “To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious, ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ. Wherefore also it is contained in the Scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief Corner-stone, elect, precious; and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. Unto you, therefore, which believe, he is precious; but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient; whereunto also they were appointed.” “The kingdom of God is like a man finding a treasure, for which with joy he selleth all.” These words set out the very way of believing: salvation is revealed in the gospel to be through Christ, and the heart values that way as satisfying. This is believing on the Son of God lifted up, which is compared to looking at the bronze serpent. It was a person’s approval of that provision that made it effective for his healing, and so it is here: “He that so believeth, setteth to his seal that God is true.” True in what? In the testimony He has given, that God has provided life for people and placed it all in Christ. “He that believeth not, maketh God a liar.” In what? In His saying that Christ is a safe and sure way to heaven. This is being pleased with that plan and resting in it, and it agrees with everything I know that is said about justifying faith in Scripture. This is the believing on Christ and on His name, the receiving of Him and resting on Him for salvation, described in our Catechism. It is believing that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the anointed One whom the Father has sealed, set apart and fitted for the work of reconciling man to God; and “he that believeth that Jesus is the Christ, is born of God.” This is to “believe with the heart, that God hath raised Christ from the dead.” The person believes that Christ died and was raised as a satisfaction for man’s sin. Devils may believe that. No, but the person I am speaking of “believeth it with the heart,” which no natural person does until a new heart is given to him. That is, he is heartily pleased and satisfied with this glorious way, and rests in it. And so faith lays itself out now and then in its actings, outgoings and exercise, according to all the covenant relationships under which Christ is held out in Scripture.

Now, I say, this faith can often be recognised, not only in these actings (a person may know whether his heart hungers after Christ, whether he flees to Him for refuge when pursued, whether he commits himself to God and so on), but also in its very nature. As it justifies, it can be recognised and known. A person may know clearly whether, out of known distress in himself, on hearing the report and fame of Christ’s fullness, his heart is pleased with God’s plan in the new covenant; whether it goes out after Christ in that design, and is pleased with Him as Lord of people’s lives, stopping and resting there and nowhere else; resting in that plan with desire and delight. This is something that can be recognised. So I urge people to examine themselves impartially. And if they find that their heart has taken hold of that plan of salvation like this and has gone out after Him as precious, let them conclude from it that they have a sure and real interest in Christ Jesus, and a good claim and title to the crown, since “he that believeth shall never perish, but have everlasting life.”

fields.title: The Faith of Hypocrites and True Saving Faith
fields.body_html:
Objection. Hypocrites and reprobates have a kind of faith and are said to believe: “Many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did. But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men.” “Then Simon the sorcerer himself believed also.” They cannot help going out after Christ and that plan of salvation when they hear of it, and they claim to do so, yet they are deluded, and so may I be.

Answer. I will say nothing of that thought in your heart by which you wonder that anyone should not be pleased with the plan of salvation by Christ and drawn out towards Him, which is a very promising thing and shows that justifying faith is in your breast. Nor will I say anything to contradict your notion that a natural person, while still natural and before he receives a new heart, can be pleased with that plan and believe it warmly with his heart, a plan that completely overturns the covenant of works and humbles man as regards any self-righteousness already attained or that he could reach; for that notion is inconsistent with many truths of Scripture. Instead I offer these distinctions between the faith of all hypocrites or reprobates and the true, saving, justifying faith we have spoken of.

1. They never take hold of Christ Jesus in that plan, and Him alone, as a sufficient covering of the eyes, as is said of Abraham to Sarah. They always hold on to something of their own, at least to help win God’s favour and salvation. Their heart still speaks as that young man’s words suggest: “What shall I do to inherit eternal life?” Besides that, they still keep their former lovers and will not break their covenants with hell and death, imagining they may have Christ with these things, all sharing their heart equally, contrary to this: “A man cannot serve two masters.” Either Christ must be judged absolute Lord, and worthy to be so, or nothing at all. And so it is clear that their heart is not laid out for that plan of salvation by Christ, whom God has made the only Lord here, and in whom all fullness shall dwell. But where justifying faith is, a person’s soul and heart take hold of Christ, and Him alone, “having no confidence in the flesh.” He trusts only in God. Here too the person gives up other lovers. As they compete with Christ, he resolves “not to be for another.” He calls Him Lord, “which a man can only do by the Spirit of Christ.”

2. Just as hypocrites and reprobates never take hold of Christ alone, so they never take hold of Christ fully, as He is anointed to be a King to rule over a person in all things, a Priest to obtain pardon and make peace for a person on every occasion, and a Prophet to be wisdom, a teacher and a counsellor to a person in every case. So they do not receive Christ, especially in the first and third offices. But where true justifying faith is, a person takes hold of Christ wholly in all His offices, judging all His will “good, holy, just, and spiritual,” and “right concerning all things,” “making mention of his righteousness only.”

The person also gives himself up to be taught by Him: “Learn of me.” So that “Christ is made” to the true believer, with his own consent, “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and complete redemption.” And although he does not have all these things consciously in exercise when his heart goes out after Christ, yet on search and testing it will be found in him as I have said.

3. Hypocrites and reprobates never take hold of Christ together with all the inconveniences that may come with following Him. They stick at that, like the scribe: “And a certain Scribe came and said unto him, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest. And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.” But where true justifying faith is, a person takes hold of Him whatever the risk. He resolves to give up everything rather than give up Christ: “We have left all, and have followed thee.” “He reckoneth all to be loss and dung, for the excellency of Christ Jesus, as his Lord, and to be found in him.”

We could give other distinctions too, such as that true faith is active, “purifying the heart,” “working by love,” while “hypocrites only cleanse the outside of the platter,” and “do all to be seen of men,” “not seeking the honour that is of God only, and so cannot believe.” We could also show that true faith is never alone in a person, but is accompanied by other saving graces. But because these things will overlap with what follows, and since we are showing here that a person may recognise his state of grace by his faith and its acting on Christ, we pass over these things for now.

fields.title: Of the New Creature
fields.body_html:
THE Second great mark of a state of grace and of a true saving interest in Jesus Christ is the new creature: “If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.” This new creation, or renewal of a person, is a very noticeable change. It is less so in those who are effectually called from the womb or in their younger years, because they have had this new creature in them from that time, so that the change at later times is not as noticeable as in those who have been regenerated and brought to Christ when they were older, and so have been more obviously under the “power of darkness” before they were “translated into the kingdom of Christ.” But in all who rightly lay claim to Christ, this new creature must be present, although some do not know the opposite character and condition from experience as much as others, because they have not been equally under the power of darkness in their practice. This new creature is called “the new man,” which shows its extent. It is not simply a new tongue or a new hand, but “a new man.” A principle of new life and motion is put into the person, which is the new heart. This new principle of life sends out acts of life, or of “conformity to the image of him who created it,” so that the person is renewed in some measure in every way. This renewal of the person who is in Christ may be summed up under these two great heads:

I. There is a renewal of the person himself, soul and body, in some measure.

1. His understanding is renewed, so that he judges “Christ preached” in the gospel to be “the wisdom and power of God,” a wise and strong plan worthy of God. He knows the things of God truly and solidly, not as yes and no and uncertain fancies, but as all yes and amen, solid, certain and substantial things that have a desirable fulfilment in Christ and come back very much to Him: “The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him; neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned: but he that is spiritual, judgeth all things.” “As God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me, and Silvanus, and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him amen, unto the glory of God by us.” Natural people brought up under gospel ordinances may have some intellectual knowledge of God, Christ, the promises, the movements of the Holy Spirit and so on, so that they can discuss, preach and argue about these things. Yet they regard them as commonly accepted maxims of Christianity, which it would be odd and disgraceful to depart from, but not as real, solid, substantial truths on which to risk their souls and their everlasting being. The understanding is also renewed to understand something of God in the creatures, as bearing marks of His glorious attributes. Such people see “the heavens declaring his glory and power.” They understand something of God in providence and in the events that happen: “His wondrous works declare that his name is near.” The understanding also perceives the conditions and states of the soul differently from before, as we find the saints usually speaking in Scripture: “O my soul, thou hast said unto the Lord, Thou art my Lord”; “My soul said, Thy face will I seek”; “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” “Return unto thy rest, O my soul.”

2. The heart and affections are renewed. The heart is made “a new heart, a heart of flesh,” able to receive impressions, with a copy of His law stamped on it and the fear of God put into it, so that the person’s duty becomes in a sense natural and congenial to him: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.” Before, it was a “heart of stone,” without the fear of God. The affections are now renewed. Love is renewed in good measure. It goes out after God: “I will love the Lord”; after His law: “O how love I thy law!”; and after those who have God’s image in them: “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” “We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.” This love for God’s people is for a pure reason, because they are the children of God and keep His statutes. It is “with a pure heart fervently,” and so it goes out to everyone the person knows or takes to be such: “I am a companion of all them that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts.” It does so in every situation and condition, even where there is nothing to make them attractive or commendable except the image of God. And this love is often so fervent that it shows itself in every relationship, so that a person looks for a godly wife, a godly master, a godly servant, a godly counsellor, if he has a choice: “Mine eyes shall be upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me: he that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me.” And “it is not quenched by many waters.” Many imperfections and weaknesses, differences of opinion and wrongs received will not entirely quench love. It also shares what is good according to its measure, as the case of the godly poor requires: “Thou art my Lord, my goodness extendeth not to thee, but to the saints.” “But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth. And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him.” The person’s hatred is also renewed and is now directed against sin: “I hate vain thoughts”; and against God’s enemies as such: “Do not I hate them that hate thee?” Joy or delight is renewed, for it runs towards God: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee”; towards His law and will: “His delight is in the law of the Lord”; and towards the godly and their fellowship: “To the saints, in whom is all my delight.” Sorrow is turned against sin, which has wronged Christ: “Looking to him whom they have pierced, they mourn.” “The sorrow is godly,” against whatever encroaches on God’s honour: “They are sorrowful for the solemn assembly, and the reproach of that is their burden.” There is some renewal in all the affections, as in every other part of the soul, now pointing towards God.

3. Even the person’s outward members are renewed, as the Scripture says: the tongue, the eye, the ear, the hand, the foot. So “those members which once were used as weapons of unrighteousness unto sin, are now used as weapons of righteousness unto holiness.”

II. A person who is in Christ is renewed in some measure in all his ways: “Behold all things are become new.” The person becomes new:

1. In what he pursues. Before, he was set on any good, though only apparent good, and at best only outward: “Many say, Who will show us any good?” But now his pursuit and business is how to “be found in Christ” on that day, or how to obey Him and “walk before him in the light of the living,” which he would choose above all the mercies that fill this earth: “The earth, O Lord, is full of thy mercy, teach me thy statutes.” Christ’s interest also becomes the person’s interest, as appears in the song of Hannah and in the song of Mary. It is remarkable to see people newly converted, who have only reached the beginnings of knowledge, concerning and involving themselves in the public affairs of Christ’s kingdom, so eager to see Him riding out prosperously and subduing the peoples under Him.

2. The person who is in Christ is renewed in his worship. He used to “serve God in the oldness of the letter,” in appearance, matching the letter of the command in outward duty, which someone in whom the old man has absolute rule can do. But now he worships God “in newness of spirit,” in a new way, in which he is “helped by the Spirit of God” beyond the reach of flesh and blood. He now “serveth the true and living God,” “in spirit and in truth,” having spiritual views of God and engaged with his very soul in the work, doing and saying things truly and not falsely when he worships, and always “desiring to approach unto him as a living God,” who hears and sees him and can accept his service. I grant that he often fails in this. Yet I may say that this is the worship he intends, and sometimes reaches, and that he does not think much of worship that is not offered to God in this way. And the sin in his holy things is not the least part of his burden and struggle. Natural people are strangers to such worship, while they babble out their vainglorious boasting like the Pharisee, “Lord, I thank thee that I am not as other men,” or worship “an unknown God.”

3. The person who is in Christ is renewed in his outward calling and work in the world. He now resolves to be diligent in it, because God has commanded it: “Not slothful in business, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord.” He resolves to keep his eye on God in it as the final goal, “doing it to his glory.” He tries to keep up some communion with God while carrying out his outward work, as Jacob does in his last will, “I have waited for thy salvation, O Lord,” and as Nehemiah did: “Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven.” So the person resolves to walk with God and “set him always before him,” though I do not deny that he often fails in this.

4. He becomes new in his relationships. He becomes a more dutiful husband, father, brother, master, servant, neighbour and so on. “Herein doth he exercise himself, to keep a conscience void of offence towards men as well as towards God,” “becoming all things to all men.”

5. He becomes new in the use of lawful freedoms. He tries to use food, drink, sleep, recreation and clothing with an eye to God, working not to come under the power of any lawful thing: “All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient; all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” Nor does he want to cause offence to others in using these things: “For meat destroy not the work of God. All things indeed are pure; but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence. It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.” “Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification; not using liberty as an occasion to the flesh.” Indeed, he tries to use all these things as a stranger on earth, so that his moderation may be seen: “Let your moderation be known unto all men.” And in these things he always looks to God as the final goal, “doing all to the glory of God.” So we may say of that person, “Old things are much passed away, all things are,” in some measure, “become new.” Whoever is such a new creature is undoubtedly in Christ.

This renewal of a person in every kind of conduct, this being under law to God in all things, is that “holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.” People may imagine things for themselves. But unless they try to prove themselves to God in everything pleasing to Him, and reach some inner testimony of sincerity in that way, they will not assure their hearts before Him. “The testimony of men’s conscience is their rejoicing.” “By this we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments.” “And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence towards God.” There is no confidence if the heart condemns. This is the new creature: a principle of new spiritual life put into the heart by God, by which the heart becomes new and puts out acts of new life throughout the whole person, as we have said, so that he points towards the whole law. 1. He points towards the commands that forbid sin. So he resolves to set himself against secret sins, and “not to lay a stumbling-block before the blind.” He sets himself against little sins, as many judge them, the least things of the law: “Whosoever shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven.” He sets himself against spiritual sins, filthiness of the spirit: “Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.” He sets himself against sins of omission as well as sins of commission, since people are to be judged by these: “Then shall he say unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was an hungered, and ye gave me no meat, I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink,” etc. He even sets himself against sins that are woven into his natural temperament and constitution, and so are like “a right eye or hand” to him: “If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee,” etc. This new principle of life, by the good hand of God, makes the person set himself against every known sin, so far as not to allow any known darkness a peaceful home: “What fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?” 2. He also points towards the commands that concern duty and the stirring up of grace in a person. It makes a person “respect all God’s known commands,” and “live godly, righteously, and soberly.” Indeed, it makes him seek a right and sincere way and manner of doing things, resolving not to give up this pursuit of conformity to God’s will while he lives on earth, but always to “press forward toward the mark, for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.” This is true holiness, very fitting for all who claim to be heirs of that holy dwelling place, in the immediate company and fellowship of a holy God: “We know that when he shall appear, we shall be like him.”

Some may think these things are high attainments and very hard to reach. I grant that this is true. But:

I. Remember that there is a very generous provision in the covenant, promised to His people, which makes things easier. The Lord has pledged “to take away the stony heart, to give a heart of flesh, a new heart, a heart to fear him for ever.” He has pledged to “put his law in men’s heart; to put his fear in their heart, to make them keep that law; to put his Spirit in them, to cause them keep it.” He has promised “to satisfy the priests with fatness,” that the souls of “the people may be satisfied with his goodness,” and to keep them and water them continually, every moment. And if He must be “inquired of to do all these things” for people, He pledges to “pour out the spirit of grace and supplication on them,” and so to teach them how to seek these things and how to set Him to work to do everything for them.

II. For the satisfaction of weaker Christians, I grant that this new creature, as we have defined and expanded it, will not be found in all its degrees in every gracious person. But it is well if:

1. There is a new man. We cannot grant less than that: “If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.” And that is the new man, which all who are savingly taught by Christ must put on: “If so be that ye have heard him, and have been taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus: That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind: and that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.” There must be some renewing after the image of God in a person’s soul and body. There must be something of every part of the person pointing towards God. I grant that not everyone can teach this to others, or discern it in himself, because many do not know the distinct parts of the soul, or the reforms proper to every part of the soul and body. Yet it will be found that there is something of this kind in them. Indeed, they have a witness to it within them, if you make the thing plain and clear to them.

2. There must be such a regard for God’s known commands that a person does not peacefully allow any known sin to live in him. For “what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?” He must not regard iniquity: “Then shall I not be ashamed when I have respect unto all thy commandments.” “If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me.” I grant that people may be ignorant of many commands and many sins, and may imagine in some cases that some sins are not hateful to God. But supposing they are instructed in these things, there can be no agreement between righteousness and unrighteousness.

3. People must point towards the whole law of God in their honest resolutions. For this is nothing other than giving the heart up to God for Him to put His law in it without exception, which is part of the covenant we are to make with God: “This is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel—I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts.” I grant that many do not know how to point towards God’s law in all their ways. But if it is made clear to them how it should be done, they will aim at it. And it is true that they will often fall short of their resolutions in practice. Yet when they have failed, they can say that they had resolved otherwise, and will still honestly and without deceit resolve to do otherwise. And it will be a grief to them that they have fallen short of their resolution when the Lord shows it to them, which He will do in due time.

4. When we are to judge our state by the new creature, we must do it at a suitable time, when we are in good condition, or at least not when we are in our worst condition. For “the flesh and spirit do lust and fight against each other,” and sometimes one prevails and sometimes the other. Now, I say, we must choose a suitable time, when the spiritual part has not been beaten and overpowered by the flesh through some temptation. For in that case the new creature is driven back in its streams and largely withdrawn to the fountain and to its settled dispositions, except in some small things that are not easily noticed, by which it resists the flesh, according to the Scripture above. For that is winter time in the soul, and we may not expect fruit, or even leaves, as in other seasons. Only here, so that profane atheists do not take advantage of this, we will say this: the flesh often prevails over the spirit in a godly person, and yet the scope, aim, tenor and main direction of his way is “in the law of the Lord”; that is his walk. Whereas the path and ordinary course of the wicked is sin, as is often hinted in the book of Proverbs. And if a godly person happens to be overcome by any sin, it is usually his sad struggle, and we suppose he keeps it still laid before God to have it put right, as David says, “Wilt thou not deliver my feet from falling?”

fields.title: The Renewed Man and the Hypocrite
fields.body_html:
Objection. Atheists and hypocrites may have great changes and renewals worked on them and in them, and I fear mine may be of that kind.

Answer. I grant that atheists and hypocrites have many things in them that look like the new creature.

I. As regards the parts of the person, they may: 1. Come to much knowledge; they are enlightened. 2. Their affections may be stirred: “They receive the word with joy, as he that received the seed into stony places.” 3. They may reach a great deal of outward reformation in the outward person, both in freedom from sin and in taking on positive duty, as the Pharisee did: “God, I thank thee that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this Publican; I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.” Indeed, 4. In their practical understanding they may judge some things of God to be excellent. The officers said that “never man spake as Christ.”

II. Hypocrites may make a great deal of profession. 1. They may talk about the law and the gospel and the covenant, as the wicked do: “What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldst take my covenant in thy mouth?” 2. They may confess sin openly to their own shame, as King Saul did: “Then said Saul, I have sinned: return, my son David; for I will no more do thee harm, because my soul was precious in thine eyes this day: behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly.” 3. They may humble themselves in sackcloth with Ahab: “And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.” 4. They may inquire busily after duty and come cheerfully to receive it: “Yet they seek me daily, and delight to know my ways, as a nation that did righteousness, and forsook not the ordinance of their God: they ask of me the ordinances of justice: they take delight in approaching to God.” 5. They may side with God’s cause in a hard and difficult time, like Demas and other hypocrites in the Acts of the Apostles, who later fell away. 6. They may give much of their goods to God and to the saints, as Ananias did, if not all their goods: “Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.” Indeed, 7. It is not impossible for some such people, when their reputation is tightly bound up in it, to “give their bodies to be burned,” as in the last place quoted.

III. Hypocrites may advance far in the common and ordinary steps of a Christian work, such as the elect have when God leads them captive. 1. They may be under great convictions of sin, as Judas was: “Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.” King Saul was often like this. 2. They may tremble at the word of God and be under much terror, as Felix was: “And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season I will call for thee.” 3. They may “rejoice in receiving of the truth, as he that received the seed into stony places.” 4. They may have some peace and quiet in expecting salvation by Christ, as the foolish virgins did. 5. All this may be supported and followed by a good measure of reformation, as with the Pharisee: “The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.” “The unclean spirit may go out of them.” 6. This work may seem to be confirmed by some special experiences and “tastings of the good word of God.”

IV. Hypocrites may have some things very like the saving graces of the Spirit. 1. They may have a kind of faith, with Simon Magus: “Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip, and wondered, beholding the miracles and signs which were done.” 2. They may have a kind of repentance and may walk mournfully: “What profit is it that we have walked mournfully before the Lord of hosts?” 3. They may have a great fear of God, such as Balaam had, who would not go with Balak’s messengers for a house full of gold without first asking God’s permission and receiving it. 4. They have a kind of hope: “The hypocrite’s hope shall perish.” 5. They have some love, as Herod had for John: “And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath’s sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her.” I need not press the point; it is beyond all question that they have counterfeits of all the saving graces.

V. They have something like the special communications of God and the witness of His Spirit, and something like “the powers of the world to come” working powerfully on them, with some flashes of joy arising from it: “For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance.” In spite of all this, they are only “almost persuaded, with Agrippa, to be Christians.” It would be tedious to speak to each of these things in detail and make it clear that they are all false and unsound. I will settle on a few things in which a truly renewed person, who is in Christ, differs from hypocrites and reprobates.

1. Whatever change there is in hypocrites, their heart is not changed and made new. The new heart is given only to the elect, when they are converted and brought under the bond of the covenant: “I will give them one heart, and one way, that they may fear me for ever.” “A new heart will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” Hypocrites never saw Christ as the only satisfying good in all the world, for which they would joyfully give up everything. For then the kingdom of God would have entered them: “The kingdom of heaven is like unto a treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.” The truly renewed person dares to say, and can say on good grounds, and has a testimony to it from on high, that his heart has been changed in taking up Christ and has been led out after Him as the only enriching treasure, in whom “to be found he accounteth all things else loss and dung.”

2. Whatever reformation or profession hypocrites reach, since it does not come from a new heart and a pure principle of zeal for God, it is always for some wicked and ulterior purpose, such as “to be seen of men,” or to escape and avoid some outward difficulty, or to be free of God’s wrath and the trouble of their own conscience: “Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge?” “What profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the Lord of hosts?” As evidence of this, they never have regard to all known commands, otherwise they would “never be ashamed.” Nor do they resolve against every known sin without deceit that their own heart recognises, otherwise they would be free of the heart’s condemning and so might rightly have “confidence before God.” If, in however small a degree, they confessed and professed Christ out of a principle of love for Him and zeal for Him, and for a right purpose, Christ would be bound by His own word “to confess them before his Father.”

3. However far hypocrites advance in the work by which people are led to Christ, they never “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.” “The one thing that is necessary,” namely Christ’s friendship and fellowship, is never their “one thing” and heart-satisfying choice; otherwise that “better part would never be taken from them.”

4. Whatever counterfeits of grace there are in hypocrites, they are all formed there without any saving work of the Spirit of Christ. And it is enough to exclude them from the benefit of this mark that they are never dead to these things or emptied of them, but always rest on them as their saviour, so that “they submit not unto the righteousness of God.” That is enough to keep them at a distance from Christ, who will never patch that old garment of hypocrites with His fine new linen, nor “put his new wine into these old bottles.”

5. We may say, Let hypocrites, reprobates or atheists have whatever they can, they lack the three great essentials of religion and true Christianity. 1. They are not broken in their hearts and emptied even of their righteousness to the point of self-loathing, while still lying open for relief. Such “lost ones Christ came to seek and save.” 2. They never took up Christ Jesus as the only treasure and jewel that alone can enrich and should satisfy. So they have never heartily agreed to God’s plan in the covenant, and so are not worthy of Him. Nor has the kingdom of God savingly entered their heart: “The kingdom of heaven is like unto a treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.” 3. They never in earnest take on Christ’s whole yoke without exception, judging all His “will just and good, holy and spiritual.” And so no rest from Christ followed for them: “Take my yoke upon you, and ye shall find rest unto your souls.” So whoever you are, if you can lay clear and rightful claim to these three things, you are beyond the reach of all the atheists, hypocrites and reprobates in the world, having answered the great purposes and intentions of the law and the gospel.

Objection. Sometimes, I think, I am clear enough to lay claim to that mark of the new creature. Yet at other times sin prevails over me so much that I am made to question all the work within me.

Answer. It is much to be lamented that people who profess His name should be so abused and enslaved by sin as many are. Yet in answer to the objection, if it is raised seriously, we say this. The saints are found in Scripture rightly laying claim to God and His covenant when sin was prevailing over them, as we find: “Iniquities prevail against me; as for our transgressions, thou shalt purge them away.” Paul “thanks God through Christ,” though he admits that “a law in his members leads him captive unto sin.” But to understand such truths better and apply them safely, we must distinguish between gross outbreaks and ordinary weaknesses or evils of the heart, sins that come on a person unawares, without forethought or any deliberation. As for the first kind, it is hard for a person, while he is under their power, to see his gracious change, even though it is in him, and very hard to draw any comfort from it until the person has to some extent recovered and begins seriously to feel such sins and resolve against them. We find David calling himself God’s servant soon after he had numbered God’s people, but he was then seriously feeling his sin: “And David’s heart smote him after that he had numbered the people. And David said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O Lord, take away the iniquity of thy servant, for I have done very foolishly.” Jonah lays claim to God as his master in the midst of his rebellion, but he is then repenting of it and in a spirit of revenge against himself for his sin. Next, as for sins of weakness and the daily intrusion of evils of the heart, they are probably the kind Paul complains of.

We will draw out some things from the seventh chapter of Romans on which Paul maintains his interest in Christ. If you can apply them to yourself, it is well. 1. When Paul finds that he fails badly and cannot reach conformity to God’s law, he does not blame the law as too strict for people to keep, as hypocrites usually say. He blames himself as being carnal, and he says of the law “that it is good, holy, and spiritual.” 2. He can say that he fell short of a good he intended and overshot himself, and that he had often honestly resolved against the evil he fell into: “For that which I do, I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I. For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good, I find not. For the good that I would, I do not; but the evil which I would not, that I do.” 3. He says that sin’s prevailing over him is his struggle, so that he judges himself wretched because of such a body of death, from which he longs to be delivered. 4. He says that while he is under the power and law of sin, there is something deep in his heart opposing it, though overpowered by it, which wants to go another way; and when that gets the upper hand, it is a delightful thing (Rom. 7:22-25). On these grounds he “thanks God in Christ that there is no condemnation to them who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.” Now then, see whether you can lay claim to these things. 1. Whether you blame yourself and approve the law while you fail. 2. Whether you can say that you often resolve against sin honestly and without known deceit, and resolve on the opposite good before the evil breaks in on you. 3. Whether you can say that you are troubled enough by your failings to judge yourself wretched because of such things, and because of a body of death, which is the root and source of such things. 4. Whether you can say that there is a part within you opposing these evils, which wants to go the right way and is, as it were, in its element when it is in God’s way. If so, it is well. Only take advice not to rest until you are to some good extent rid of the grounds of this objection, or at least until you can say very clearly that you are waging war on these things. Now a good help against the prevailing power of sin is to cling closely to Christ Jesus by faith. Faith is a desirable part of sanctification, a high degree of conformity to God’s will, and most serviceable to His design in the gospel: “The life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. I do not frustrate the grace of God.” So it should be pursued earnestly by people as a work pleasing to God: “This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent.” And so it is the ready way to draw life and nourishment from Christ, the blessed root, for fruitfulness in every situation: “Abide in me, and I in you: as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine, no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit; for without me ye can do nothing.”

fields.title: The Special Communications of God
fields.body_html:
Objection. I DO not share in those special communications of God mentioned in Scripture, or in those workings and outgoings of His Spirit that gracious people often speak of and reach. The lack of these things makes me strongly suspect my state.

Answer. I will briefly look at some of these excellent communications, and I hope that once they are rightly understood, little ground will be found for the anxious complaints of many gracious people.

1. Besides the convictions of the Spirit of God that usually prepare Christ’s way into people’s souls, and those that ordinarily accompany them afterwards, Scripture speaks of a seal of the Spirit of God. The main thing in it is the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit, imprinting the outlines and features of God’s image and revealed will on a person, as a seal or signet leaves an impression and stamp of its likeness on the thing sealed. So it is written: “The foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his; and, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.” In this way I understand the seal to be called “a witness”: “He that believeth hath the witness in himself.” That is, the grounds on which an interest in Christ is to be shown and proved are in every believer. For he has something of the sanctifying work of God’s Spirit in him, which is a sure witness, though not always a clear and evident one.

II. Christians talk a great deal about communion with God, by which they mean the felt presence of God refreshing the soul greatly. But strictly speaking, communion with God is a mutual interest between God and a person who has taken hold of Him in Christ. It is a sharing, a common interest, between God and a person. Not only does a person have an interest in God Himself and in everything that is the Lord’s, but the Lord also has a special interest in the person and in everything that belongs to him. There is a communion between husband and wife by which each has a special interest in the other’s person, goods and concerns. So it is here. There is such a communion with God: He is our God, and all things are ours because He is ours. All true believers have this communion with God at all times, as we will show later. I grant that there is an active use of that communion, by which people boldly make free with anything that belongs to God, and with God Himself as their own, with great homeliness and familiarity, especially in worship, when the soul converses with a living God, shares in the divine nature, grows like Him, travels sweetly through His attributes, and views these things, with some confidence of having an interest in them, as its own goods and property. This we call communion with God in the ordinances. This indeed is not so usually or frequently made clear to people, and not all His people share in it equally. And it is true that what is in God does not, as they perceive it, go out for a person’s benefit equally at all times. Yet communion with God properly so called, namely that common interest between God and a person who is savingly in covenant with Him, certainly always stands firm and sure. And all believers have this much communion with God in the ordinances: that their heart converses with a living God there now and then and is in some measure changed into that same image. There need be no further doubt about it.

III. There is what is called fellowship with God, which is also often misunderstood among believers. If by fellowship we mean walking in our duty as in the sight of a living God, who sees and hears us and witnesses all our conduct, it is something common to all gracious people. They all have it as a settled habit and in intention: “I have set the Lord always before me.” Indeed, they often have it actively in exercise when their spirit is in any good frame. They walk as if they saw God standing beside them, and have some thought of His favour through Christ: “Truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ.” If by fellowship we mean a sweet, refreshing, familiar, felt conversing with God that delights and refreshes the soul beyond what a sense of duty does, then it is a walking in the light of His face, and a good part of felt presence. And although it seems Enoch had much of it, since it is said, “He walked with God,” it is not as general as the first kind, nor as common to all Christians. For here the soul is filled as with marrow and fatness, following hard after its guide and remarkably upheld by His right hand: “My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips. My soul followeth hard after thee, thy right hand upholdeth me.”

IV. There is what is called access to God. I take this to be the removal of obstacles in the way between a person and God, so that the person is admitted to come near. We are said to have access to a great person when the doors are thrown open, the guards around him are removed and we are admitted to come close to him. So it is here. Now this access is sometimes taken in Scripture to mean Christ’s preparing the way, the removal of hostility between God and sinners, so that people now have an open way to come to God through Christ: “For through him we both have an access by one Spirit unto the Father.” Sometimes it is taken to mean the active use of that access bought by Christ, when a person finds that all the obstacles and differences that ordinarily come between him and God are removed. God is not reserved towards him, or like a stranger, keeping Himself back from him or frowning on him. Instead the person is admitted to “come even to his seat.” Job complains of the lack of this when he says, “Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him: on the left hand, where he doth work, but I cannot behold him: he hideth himself on the right hand, that I cannot see him.” The first kind of access is common to all believers. They are brought near by the blood of the covenant and are no longer far off, since the deadly hostility between God and them has been removed. But access in the other sense is given out more according to the Lord’s absolute sovereignty and pleasure. And it is within believers’ power to block it for themselves, until it pleases the Lord mercifully and freely to grant it to them again. So it goes up and down, and there need be no question about a person’s state because of it.

V. There is what is called liberty before God, which properly means freedom, or free speaking to God. Many seriously question their state because they lack this now and then, since Scripture says, “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.” But they wrongly restrict the liberty spoken of there to this free speaking before God. I grant that where the Spirit of the Lord savingly reveals God’s will in the Scriptures to a person, there is liberty from any obligation to the ceremonial law, from the condemning power of the moral law, and from much of the gross darkness and ignorance that lies on natural people’s hearts like a veil, hiding Christ in the gospel from them. I grant too that sometimes the godly are also given this liberty, which is a free communing with God, an “ordering of our cause before him, and filling of our mouth with arguments,” but not in the same way as liberty in the senses just mentioned. Although the Lord has bound Himself to “pour out the spirit of prayer upon all the house of David” in some measure, this communication of the Spirit which we call liberty, or free speaking to God, depends very much on the Lord’s absolute pleasure as to when and in what measure He allows it. This liberty, which we call freedom or free speaking with God in prayer, is sometimes largely withheld from any great confidence during prayer, at least until it draws near the end. It consists largely in a liveliness of the understanding to grasp the case a person is to speak about before God, so that he can set out his cause. Next, there are words or spoken expressions that are fine, fitting and very forceful, powerful and pointed. Joined with this there is also a fervency of spirit in prayer, which Scripture speaks of; the soul is warm, bent on it and very intent. Usually in this liberty there is also a special melting of the heart, often joined with a great measure of the “spirit of grace and supplication,” so that the soul is poured out before God as for a firstborn. Such is the liberty many saints receive before God, when in great brokenness of heart and fervency of spirit they are admitted to speak their mind fully to God as a living God who at least takes notice of their prayer. Sometimes this liberty is joined with confidence, and then it is not only a free but also a bold speaking before God. It is that “boldness with confidence”: “In whom we have boldness and access with confidence, by the faith of him.” This is more rarely given to people than the first kind, yet it is ordinary. Besides what we mentioned before, it includes some influence of the Spirit on faith, making it act vigorously in prayer. There is a sweet, mournful frame of spirit in which a person pours out his heart into God’s bosom and, with some confidence of His favour and goodwill, pleads his cause before Him as a living God. This is all the felt presence that many saints reach. There is no ground for doubting a person’s state on the point of liberty before God in this last sense, because there is nothing essential to a state of grace in it. Some have it and some lack it; some have it at some times and not at others, so that it goes up and down a great deal. Yet I may say that gracious people can do much, with a very ordinary influence, to help reach and keep such a frame of spirit.

VI. There is what is called influence, or the breathing of the Spirit. This gracious influence (for I am speaking only of this kind now) is either ordinary, consisting of the workings of the Holy Spirit on the soul and on the settled graces there, by which they are kept alive and in some exercise and action, though not very noticeably. I think this influence always goes with believers, and is that “keeping and watering night and day, and every moment.” Or this influence is more unusual and special, and is to a gracious but withered soul what “wind and breath were to the dry bones,” putting them in good condition, and “as the dew or rain to the grass,” or to a newly mown field and parched ground. Such influence is meant by the “blowing of the south wind, making the spices to flow out.” When the Spirit moves like this, an edge is put on the graces of God in the soul and they are made to act more vigorously. This is the “enlarging of the heart,” by which a “man doth run in the ways of God.” This influence is more noticeable than the first kind and not so ordinarily given. Here too the wind sometimes blows more on one grace and sometimes more noticeably on another, and often on many graces together. And according to the smaller or greater measure of this influence, the soul acts more or less vigorously towards God. And since faith is a created grace in the soul, this influence of the Spirit rests on it, sometimes less and sometimes more, and the assurance of faith is small or great accordingly.

VII. Scripture often speaks of the hearing of prayer, and many trouble themselves about it, claiming they know nothing of it from experience. I grant that there is a favourable hearing of prayer, but we must remember that it is of two kinds. Either: 1. It is such that a person is simply to believe it, by reasoning on Scriptural grounds. For example, if I have fled to Christ and come to God in Him, praying according to His will, not regarding iniquity in my heart, and exercising faith about the thing I pray for, absolutely or conditionally according to the nature of the thing and the promises about it, then I am bound to believe that God hears my prayer and will give what is good, according to these Scriptures: “Whatsoever ye ask in my name, I will do it.”—“This is our confidence, that whatsoever we ask according to his will, he heareth us.”—“Believe that ye receive, and ye shall have what ye desire.” “If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear.” So if I do not regard iniquity, I may believe that He hears me. Or: 2. A person perceives by feeling that God hears his prayer. It is made clear to his heart without any logical deduction. Hannah received such a hearing of prayer: “Her countenance was no more sad.” Surely the Lord breathed on her faith and made her believe that she was heard. She could not prove it by any argument, for she had no grounds on which to build the premises of such an argument from Scripture in that particular case. God stamped it on her heart in some felt way and so made her believe it. This is only rarely granted, especially in cases that can clearly be deduced from Scripture. So people should be well satisfied with exercising their faith about the first kind, and ought to leave it to God to give as much of the second as He pleases. A person’s state of grace should not be called into question because of such hearing of prayer.

VIII. There is assurance of God’s favour through the witness of our own spirits. This assurance is drawn by reasoning in a logical argument, like this: Whoever believes on Christ will never perish. But I believe on Christ. Therefore I will never perish. Whoever has regard to all God’s commandments will never be ashamed. But I have regard to all His commands. Therefore I will never be ashamed. I say that by reasoning like this, and comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, a person may reach good certainty about his state of grace. It is taken for granted that “by loving the brethren in deed and in truth we may assure our hearts before God,” and that a person may rejoice in the testimony of a good conscience: “A man may have confidence towards God, if his heart do not condemn him.” So we may reach some assurance, though not full assurance, by the witness of our own spirits. I do not deny that in this witnessing of our spirits about assurance there is some working together of the Spirit of God. But I think it needs only a very ordinary influence, without which we can do nothing. Now this assurance, such as it is, may be reached by intelligent believers who keep a good conscience in their walk. So I hope there need be no argument about it as far as a person’s state of grace is concerned. For if a person will clear himself of his heart’s condemning, he will quickly reach this assurance.

IX. There is a “witnessing of God’s Spirit,” mentioned as “bearing witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.” This working of the Spirit is best understood if we set out a logical argument by which our spirit bears witness to our sonship. For example: Whoever loves the brothers has passed from death to life and so is in Christ. But I love the brothers. Therefore I have passed from death to life. Here there is a threefold working of the Spirit, or rather three workings. The first is a beam of divine light on the first premise, convincing a person of its divine authority as the word of God. The Spirit of the Lord must bear witness to the divine origin of the Scriptures, that they are the infallible word of God, far beyond all the other arguments that can be used for it. The second working is a glorious beam of light from the Spirit shining on the second premise, and so on His own graces in the soul, revealing them to be true graces and such as Scripture calls true. In this way we are said to “know by his Spirit the things that are freely given unto us of God.” The third working is connected with the third part of the argument, the conclusion. I think this is nothing other than an influence on faith, strengthening it to draw a conclusion of full assurance from those premises.

Now, deferring to others who have greater light in the Scripture and more experience of these precious communications, I think that the witness of the Spirit, or His witnessing, mentioned in “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit that we are the children of God,” is not that first working on the first premise. For that working is the testimony of the Spirit by which He bears witness to the divine origin of the whole of Scripture and asserts its divine authority to the souls of gracious people. Such a working may rest on a truth of Scripture that has nothing to do with a person’s sonship or interest in Christ. The Spirit may shine on any truth relating to duty, or any other fundamental truth, impressing its divine origin on the soul, and say nothing about a person’s interest in Christ. Nor is the third working of the Spirit, by which He makes faith boldly draw the conclusion, this witnessing of the Spirit. For that working is nothing other than an influence on faith, bringing it out to full assurance. But what this full assurance is drawn from is something already confirmed and witnessed. So I think the second working of the Spirit, on the second premise and so on the graces in the person, is that witness of God’s Spirit: that beam of divine light shining on those graces, by which they are made very clear to the understanding. That is the witness; His shining on them like this is His witnessing. For only here, in this premise and in this working, does the Spirit of God prove to be a fellow witness with our spirit. The main thing in which the witness of our spirit consists lies in the second premise, and so the Spirit of God’s witnessing with our spirits lies in that same premise. So these two witnesses confirm and bear witness to one and the same thing, namely the truth and reality of such and such graces in the person. Our own spirit or conscience testifies to it according to its knowledge, and the Spirit of the Lord certainly affirms and witnesses that it is so. Then a sentence is drawn out, a conclusion of the person’s sonship, by the person’s faith, which the Spirit breathes on for that purpose. And this conclusion carries the full assurance of a person’s sonship. It may be presumed that some true saints do not share in this all their days: “And deliver them, who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.”

X. I speak with the experience of many saints, and I hope according to Scripture, when I say that there is a communication of the Spirit of God, sometimes given to some of His people, that is something besides, if not beyond, the witnessing of sonship spoken of before. It is a glorious divine showing of God to the soul, pouring out God’s love in the heart. It is something better felt than described. It is no audible voice, but it is a flash of glory filling the soul with God, as He is life, light, love and liberty, equal to that audible voice, “O man, greatly beloved,” and putting a person into raptures, with this on his heart: “It is good to be here.” It is what went out from Christ to Mary when He simply spoke her name: “Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni, which is to say, Master.” He had spoken some words to her before, and she did not realise it was He. But when He uttered this one word, MARY, some wonderful divine communication and showing was made to her heart, by which she was so satisfyingly filled that there was no room for arguing and disputing whether it was Christ or not, or whether she had any interest in Him. That showing produced faith in itself and won credit and trust for itself, and was equal to “Thus saith the Lord.” This is such a glimpse of glory that it may in the highest sense be called “the earnest,” or first fruits, “of the inheritance.” For it is a felt showing of the holy God, almost wholly conforming the person to His likeness, swallowing him up so that he forgets everything except the present showing. Oh, how glorious is this showing of the Spirit! Here faith rises to such full assurance that it passes wholly into the felt presence of God. This is what best deserves the name of felt presence. It is probably not given to all believers, some of whom “are all their days under bondage, and in fear.” But here love, almost perfect, casts “out fear.” This is given so entirely at the Master’s pleasure, and is so fleeting, passing or quickly gone when it does come, that no one may call his state of grace into question for lack of it.

XI. There is what we call peace, about which many trouble themselves. This peace concerns either a person’s state, that he is reconciled to God through Jesus Christ, or his present situation and condition, that he is walking in a way approved by God, at least so far that there is no quarrel or dispute between God and him threatening a blow. Both of these exist either in the court of Scripture, and so in God’s reckoning, or in the court of a person’s own conscience. Peace about a person’s state, as being in Christ, is sure in the court of Scripture and of heaven when a person takes hold of Christ by faith and has the new creature: “Being justified by faith, we have peace with God.” Since it is sure and solid in the court of Scripture, it should hold sure in the court of a person’s conscience, if the conscience is rightly informed, for in that case it always speaks according to Scripture. But because the conscience is often misinformed and in the dark, there is often peace about a person’s state according to Scripture while his conscience threatens the opposite, keeps condemning, and refuses to acquit the person as reconciled to God through Christ. In this case the conscience must be informed, and the person’s state of grace made clear by the marks of grace, as we showed before. Here the witness of my own spirit will do much to quieten the cry of the conscience. And if the Spirit of the Lord adds His witness and testimony, the conscience is perfectly satisfied and proclaims peace to the person.

The other peace, about a person’s present situation or condition, that it is approved by God in a gospel sense, may be lacking, and rightly lacking, even when peace about a person’s state is sure. This peace about a person’s situation and condition exists first in the court of Scripture. This is when a person is not regarding iniquity and has regard to God’s commands without exception. Then Scripture says that he stands on level ground and need fear no settled quarrel between God and him leading to a temporal blow. When this is the case, his conscience should also acquit him in the same way, and would do so if it were rightly informed. But because the conscience is often in the dark, a person may be alarmed with evil in the court of conscience, as if he could rightly expect a blow from God because of his sin and some quarrel God has with him, although God intends salvation for him. This is enough to keep a person disquieted and to deprive him of the rejoicing allowed to him while he is walking in his integrity. So here too a person must inform his conscience, and accept no accusations or condemnations from it unless it makes them clear from Scripture. Let everyone stand at that bar, both concerning his state and concerning his condition or situation. Let him appeal from all other courts to that one, and accept no charge except what agrees with the truth of God, by which the conscience is to proceed in all things. If this were well attended to, there would not be so many groundless suspicions among the Lord’s people about either their state or their condition, at every thought that enters their minds.

XII. There is the joy of the Holy Spirit. This is when the Spirit breathes on our rejoicing in God, which is a grace very little exercised by many, and makes it come out noticeably and vigorously. He excites and stirs up the passion of joy and delight in the soul, so that there is an “unspeakable and glorious joy in the soul” at the sense of God’s friendship and of nearness to Him: “In whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.” This joy follows peace, and peace follows righteousness: “The kingdom of God—is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.” This joy will generally match the measure of the assurance of faith, as it says, “In whom believing, ye rejoice.” So removing mistakes about the other things will quieten doubts about this one.

Now because some of these excellent communications of the Spirit are called into question as delusions of Satan after they have gone, we say this to vindicate them. The special workings of God’s Spirit in any high degree are usually given to people after brokenness of spirit: “Make me to hear joy and gladness, that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice.” Or after unusual effort in religious duty: “And I set my face unto the Lord God, to seek by prayer and supplication, with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes.—And whiles I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin—the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me.” Or in a time of much suffering for righteousness: “Rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ’s sufferings; that when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy. If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the Spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you.” Or if they break in like the rain that does not wait for man, then they so humble and abase the person: “Woe is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips—for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts.” And so many evidences of grace are found in the person: “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.” Or these things so stir a person up to holiness, and to have everything answer to and agree with these showings of God: “Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.” The person under them loathes everything except God’s friendship and fellowship: “Peter said unto Jesus, Lord, it is good for us to be here.” And while they are in the soul, these things carry so much authority and divine signature on them and with them that afterwards they may sufficiently appear to be special communications of God and remarkable gracious workings of His Spirit. They are no delusions of “Satan transforming himself into an angel of light,” nor the kind of common flashes of the Spirit that may later allow an irrecoverable falling away from God: “For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come; if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance.”

Now then, to conclude this part of the work, which concerns the testing, I say this to all who complain of lacking the precious outpourings of the Spirit. 1. Bless God if you lack nothing essential for showing a saving interest in Christ. God has given you Christ Jesus, the greatest gift He had. And since your heart is laid out for Him, He will give you with Him all things that are good for you in their season. 2. I believe that on strict search and testing, once you have understood the communications of the Spirit, you are not as great a stranger to many things as you suspected. But 3. Remember that the promises of life and peace with God are nowhere in Scripture made to those special things you say you lack. The promises are made to faith followed by holiness. And it may be presumed that many heirs of glory do not share in some of these things in this life, but “are in bondage all their days through fear of death.” So there should be no mistake about these things. We may seek after them, but God is free to give or withhold them. 4. Many seek such showings before they give credit by faith to God’s word. He has testified that there is life enough for people in Christ Jesus. If people would set their seal to it by believing that God is true, they would share in more of these excellent things. 5. I may say that many do not have honourable views and thoughts of the Spirit of God, whose proper work it is to put out these noble workings. They do not adore Him as God, but vex, grieve, quench and resist Him. And many people who complain of lacking these things do not take the trouble to seek the Spirit in His outgoings, and few set themselves apart to receive such precious things. So take more trouble in religion, give more credit to His word, and think more highly of the Spirit of God, and so you may find more of these excellent things.

fields.title: Things Premised for the More Ignorant
fields.body_html:
TO understand this better, we will first set down some things for the information of those who are less instructed, and then speak more directly to the matter. As for the things to set down first:

1. In the beginning the Lord, out of His generosity, made a covenant with man in Adam: “And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” And He enabled man to remain in that covenant: “God hath made man upright.” But man, by eating that forbidden fruit, broke that covenant: “They, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant.” He made it void for ever: “By the deeds of the law, there shall no flesh be justified in his sight.” And by it he plunged himself into every misery: “As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned.”

2. From all eternity the Lord most freely purposed and intended to save people another way, namely by Christ Jesus and the covenant of grace. In it He intended reconciliation with the elect through Christ Jesus, God and man, born of a woman in due time, to make this agreement effective. He first made this plan of satisfying His own justice and saving the elect through Christ known to our first parents in paradise, where He says, “That the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent’s head.” And in every generation the Lord has made this known to His church.

3. In every age the Lord has covenanted to be the reconciled God of all those who, by submitting to His ordinances, professed their satisfaction with this plan and bound themselves to rest in it and to seek salvation by Christ Jesus, as God offers Him in the gospel. So all the people of Israel are called the Lord’s people, and are said to declare Him to be their God, and He declares them to be His people: “Thou hast avouched the Lord this day to be thy God, and to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and to hearken unto his voice: and the Lord hath avouched thee this day to be his peculiar people, as he hath promised thee, and that thou shouldest keep all his commandments.” Indeed, the Lord also pledges Himself to be the God of the offspring and children of those who submit themselves to His ordinances in this way. The covenant is said to be made between God and all the people, young and old, present and not present that day, and all are appointed to come under some seal of that covenant, as Abraham was commanded. This was so not only in the Old Testament, but it is so in the New Testament too. The Lord offers Himself to be our God in Christ Jesus. And when people profess their satisfaction with that offer, and as evidence of it submit themselves to the ordinances, they are counted a covenanted people and are joined to His church by thousands, receiving a seal of the covenant without any further particular prior examination: “Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of sins. Then they that gladly received the word were baptized; and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.”

4. Many deal treacherously with God in this covenant: “Nevertheless, they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues; for their heart was not right with him, neither were they stedfast in his covenant.” Although they profess their high regard for Christ the Saviour and their heartfelt satisfaction with that plan of saving sinners by Him and having the image of God restored in them by Him, their heart is not right with God, and they content themselves with an empty title of being in a sealed covenant with God. “Abraham is our father,” they say. For although the Lord obliges everyone who professes satisfaction with Christ Jesus, the ransom He devised, to be hearty and sincere in it, and makes the spiritual promises of the covenant good only to those who are, since only they are “privileged to be the sons of God, who do really receive Christ,” yet the Lord allows many, in both the Old and New Testaments, to profess that they have taken hold of Him in Christ while their heart is not engaged. And He admits them as members of His church, granting them the use of the ordinances and many other outward mercies and privileges denied to the heathen, who are not in covenant with Him.

5. Although most people foolishly imagine that they have taken hold of God in Christ Jesus sincerely and heartily, or at least, without any grounds or warrant, promise themselves a new heart before they die, very few really and heartily take hold of God in Christ Jesus as He is offered in the gospel. And so very few are saved, as is clear: “Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way which leadeth unto life, and few there be who find it.” “Many are called, but few are chosen.” If people would believe this, it might help to alarm them.

6.
