No one at all heartily takes hold of God in Christ Jesus and rests in that ransom God has found, except those who are elected: “But the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded.” And it is their hearts that the Lord sovereignly settles on that blessed choice: “No man can come to me, except the Father, which hath sent me, draw him.” Yet the Lord has left it as a duty on people who hear this gospel to take hold of His offer of salvation through Christ Jesus, as if it were in their power to do it. And through these commands and appeals, in which He binds people to the thing, the Lord conveys life and strength to the elect, and in them conveys the new heart to those who heartily embrace God’s plan of saving sinners and receive Christ in His covenant relationships. Or, it is the Lord’s purpose in these commands and invitations to set people to some duty, with which He usually works together to accomplish that end between Him and them. So it is a coming on our part, and yet a drawing on His part: “No man can come to me, except the Father, which hath sent me, draw him.” It is a drawing on His part and a running on ours: “Draw me, we will run after thee.” It is an approaching on our part, and yet a “choosing and causing to approach” on His part. It is a believing or receiving on our part: “But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” And yet “it is given us to believe.”

fields.title: Closing with God's Device of Saving Sinners
fields.body_html:
HAVING set these things down, I say this: if people do not find in themselves the marks of a saving interest in Christ spoken of in the first part of the treatise, then to make their state secure they are bound, with all diligence, personally and heartily to accept and take hold of God’s plan of saving sinners by Christ Jesus, held out in the gospel.

In dealing with this, we will:

I. Show what it is to accept and take hold of that noble plan.

II. Show that it is the necessary duty of those who want to be in favour with God and make their souls secure.

III. Show what is required beforehand of those who carry out this duty.

IV. Show what the qualities and properties of this duty are, if it is rightly carried out.

V. Show what its natural consequences are, if it is performed rightly.

I. As for the First, what it is to take hold of God’s plan of saving sinners by Christ Jesus, held out in the gospel. Here we must remember, as we showed before, that at first God willed man to remain in His favour by holding fast to the original integrity in which he was created. But man by his sin lost God’s favour, made that covenant of works void, and put himself in a state of complete inability to regain the Lord’s friendship that he had lost by his sin, to rescue himself from the curse and wrath now due to him for sin, or in any way to bring about his own salvation. But the Lord has freely revealed another way of restoring man’s lost state, namely by sending His Son Christ Jesus in the flesh to satisfy His justice for the sins of the elect, to restore His image, now defaced, in them, and to bring them to glory. And He has made an open proclamation in the church that whoever will lay aside all thoughts of saving themselves by the covenant of works, or by their own righteousness, and will heartily agree to be saved by Christ Jesus, shall be restored to a better condition than man was in before, and shall be saved. So then, to take hold of God’s plan of saving sinners by Christ Jesus is to give up and abandon all thought of help towards salvation from our own righteousness, and to agree to this way that God has found. It is to value and highly esteem Christ Jesus as the treasure that is enough to make poor man rich, and with the heart to believe this testimony, that there is life enough in Him for people. It is to be pleased with this plan and rest in it as the only way to true happiness. It is to point towards this Mediator as God holds Him out in the gospel, with a desire to lay the weight of our whole state on Him. This is what is called faith, or believing, the “receiving of Christ,” or “believing on his name.” This is the “believing on the Lord Jesus Christ” that the jailer was commanded for his safety. It agrees with all the descriptions of justifying faith in the Scripture. It answers to the type of “looking to the brazen serpent lifted up in the wilderness.” It is assumed in all the ordinary actings of faith to which promises are attached in Scripture. It will be found in all who have received the new heart from God, and in no one else.

II. As for the Second thing, that this is the necessary duty of all who want to be in favour with God and make their souls secure, it appears like this:

1. This taking hold of God’s plan, or believing in Christ, is commanded everywhere in Scripture by the Lord as the condition of the new covenant, giving title and right to all the spiritual blessings of the covenant. For it is in substance the receiving of Christ. It is commanded when God tells people to “come and buy,” that is, to make everything their own by taking hold of that plan: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” The weary are commanded to come to Him in this way for their rest: “This is his commandment, that we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ.” This is enough to prove it a binding duty. But further, it is a duty that alone gives title and right to sonship. For only those who receive Him are given the privilege of being sons: “But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.”

2. It appears to be the necessary duty of all like this: nothing less than this gives God His opportunity, when He offers Himself to be our God in Christ; and nothing less than this matches our profession, as we are in covenant with Him as members of His visible church. The Lord offers to be our God in Christ. If we do not take hold of the offer, laying aside all thoughts of other ways by which we might reach happiness, we give Him no opportunity. He says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.” If we do not take hold of the offer, we give God no answer. Moreover, we are all “baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, for the remission of sins.” Now unless we take hold of Christ, as we said, we make that profession false. So since this is what answers God’s offer in the gospel and makes good our profession as members of His church, it is a necessary duty laid on us.

3. Whatever else a person has, if he does not take hold of God’s plan concerning Christ Jesus like this and does not receive Him, it is of no use, either for the acceptance of his person or of his performances, or for the saving of his soul. People are accepted only in Christ the beloved: “To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the Beloved.” Abel and his offering are accepted by faith: “Without faith it is impossible to please God”; and “He that believeth not is condemned already, and shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.” Without this, no outward title is of any use: “the children of the kingdom are cast out” if this is lacking. The people of Israel are like the other heathen as regards a graceless state, lying “open to the wrath of God”: “Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will punish all them which are circumcised with the uncircumcised; Egypt, and Judah, and Edom: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.” If people do not believe that He who was killed at Jerusalem, who was called Christ Jesus, testified to by the prophets and declared to be the Son of God by many mighty works, I say, if people do not believe that He is the way and do not take hold of Him as the only way, they will die in their sins: “I said therefore unto you, that ye shall die in your sins: for if ye believe not that I am he, ye shall die in your sins.”

We say, then, that it is a most necessary duty to take hold of Christ Jesus like this, as the blessed relief appointed for sinners. Everyone who has come to years of understanding and hears this gospel is bound to take to heart his own lost condition and God’s gracious offer of peace and salvation through Christ Jesus, and to flee quickly from the wrath to come by accepting and taking hold of this offer, resting in it heartily as a satisfying way of saving lost sinners. And so that everyone may be more encouraged to set about this duty when they hear Him begging them to be reconciled to Him, let them remember that peace and salvation are offered to the people in universal terms, to all without exception. “If any man will,” he shall be welcome. If anyone thirsts, even after something that will never profit, they will still be welcome here, on the condition mentioned above: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money: come ye, buy and eat: yea, come buy wine and milk without money, and without price. Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? Hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.” All are “commanded to believe.” “This is his commandment, that we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ.” The promises are to all who are outwardly called by the gospel. God excludes no one, unless they exclude themselves: “The promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.” So if anyone has a mind for it, they may come forward; “he will in nowise cast them out,” being “able to save to the uttermost them who come to God through him.” And those who have long delayed taking this matter to heart have all the more need to see to it now, in case the things that belong to their peace are hidden from their eyes. But all these words will have no effect on people until “God pour out his Spirit from on high” to make people draw near to God in Christ. Yet we must still press people’s duty on them, and beg and charge them, by the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ and the account they must give Him on that day, to give the Lord no rest until He sends out that “Spirit, which he will give to them who ask it,” and makes them know what belongs to their peace and brings them to their duty.

fields.title: What Is Required of Those Who Would Believe
fields.body_html:
III. WE come now to speak of the Third thing, what is required beforehand of those who are to carry out this duty. People must not rush into this matter rashly, thoughtlessly and ignorantly, saying they are pleased with that plan of saving sinners by Christ and will rest in Him and rely on Him for safety. People often deceive themselves here and imagine they have done the thing. So we will set out some things required beforehand in a person who is to take hold of Christ Jesus. We do not offer them as positive qualifications that make a person fit for Christ (“Come—without money, and without price”). Yet they are things without which a person cannot knowingly and heartily carry out the duty of believing on Christ Jesus.

There are the common principles that can be assumed in those who live under gospel ordinances: the knowledge that people have immortal souls; that soul and body will be united again on the last day; that there is a heaven and a hell, one of which will be everyone’s everlasting portion; that the Old and New Testaments are the true word of God and the rule of faith and conduct; that everyone by nature is without the grace of God, an enemy of God and an heir of condemnation; that reconciliation is only through the Mediator Christ Jesus; that faith unites us to Him and is the condition of the new covenant; and that holiness is the fruit of true faith and is to be pursued, since without it no one will see God. Besides these things, the knowledge of which is necessary, I say this is required of the person who wants to believe on Christ Jesus:

First, he must take his natural condition to heart. Here he must know some things and also be very serious about them. I say he must know some things, such as these:

1. That just as he was born a rebel and outlaw against God, so he has disobeyed God by many actual sins and confirmed the loss of His favour. Indeed, a person should know many particular instances of his rebellion in every area: that he is a liar, a Sabbath-breaker, a blasphemer or the like, as Paul afterwards speaks very specifically about himself: “Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious.”

2. The person must know that the wrath of God pronounced in Scripture stands in force against the very sins he is guilty of, and so he is undoubtedly the one against whom God, who cannot lie, has declared war. A person must know that when the Scripture says, “Cursed is he that offereth a corrupt thing unto God,” it speaks against him for the superficial service he has offered God with the outward person while his heart was far away. When the word says, “The Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain,” the person must know it speaks against him, for he has often carelessly profaned that dreadful name “before which all knees should bow,” and “which his enemies do take in vain.” When the word says, “Cursed is he that doth the work of the Lord negligently,” the person must know that it speaks against him, for he has heard the word preached irreverently, with much wandering of heart and drowsiness, and has often prayed before Him without feeling, faith or understanding. When the word says, “Woe be unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, and putteth his bottle to him, to make him drunk also, that he may look on his nakedness,” the person must know that it is spoken against him, for he has boasted of making his neighbour drunk, and dreadful wrath is decreed by the Lord against him according to that Scripture. When the word says, “God will judge unclean persons,” and will shut them out of the “New Jerusalem, and they shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone,” the person must know that the Scripture speaks these very words against him, since he is an unclean person. So he is the one against whom the curses of the law strike directly.

3. A person must know that he has nothing of his own with which to obtain his peace and free himself from the danger he is in, because “all his righteousness is as an unclean thing.” His prayers, his other service done to God, his giving to the poor and so on are not acceptable to God, since they did not come from a right principle in his heart and were not done in a right way, for a right reason or for a right purpose. His “sacrifices have been an abomination unto God.”

4. He must know that just as he is without all the saving graces of the Spirit, such as the true love of God, the true fear of His name, godly sorrow for sin and so on, so in particular he lacks faith in Christ, who takes away the sins of all who believe on Him. Until a person knows this, he will always leave all his debt and burden, without care or concern, anywhere else rather than bring it to the guarantor.

Now not only must a person know these things, as I said before, but he must also take them very seriously to heart. That is, he must be moved by these things and be in real earnest about them, as he usually is in other matters where he is most serious. Indeed, he should be more in earnest here than in other matters, because it concerns him more. This seriousness produces:

First, a taking of salvation to heart more than anything else. Are people bound to “seek first the kingdom of God”? Is there only “one thing necessary”? Does Paul “count all things loss and dung” for this matter? Is a person a gainer, “gaining all the world, if he lose his soul”? Is this to be the only ground of joy, “that men’s names are written in the book of life”? And will people who want to be counted serious not take their soul and salvation more to heart than anything else? Surely it cannot be otherwise. Let no one deceive themselves. If the danger to their soul, its salvation, and how to be in favour with God have not gone nearer to their heart than anything else in the world, it cannot be supposed on just grounds that they ever knew sin, or God, or the eternity of His wrath rightly.

Second, this seriousness breaks the person’s heart, makes its stubbornness faint and leads it out to sorrow, as one sorrows for a firstborn. I grant that their sorrow will fit that Scripture better later on, when they see Christ pierced by their sins.

Third, it leads the person to self-loathing. A person who sees himself like this cannot help loathing himself for the abominations by which he has destroyed himself. There is something of that spirit of revenge mentioned as a fruit of true repentance: “This self-same thing that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you—yea, what revenge!”

Fourth, this seriousness makes the person determined to find relief. Since it is not in himself, he dares not put off and delay his business as before. And this is indeed required: that he finds himself so pursued and pressed that he flees somewhere for refuge. I grant that some have a higher and some a lower degree of this seriousness, as we showed in the first part of this treatise. But if we speak of the Lord’s ordinary way of working with those who have come of age, we say that they must take their soul’s state very seriously to heart, despairing of help in themselves, “since the whole need not a physician, but those who are sick.” As for the measure, we plead only for what would probably lead a person to deal heartily with Christ on whatever terms He offers Himself to be taken hold of.

The second thing required beforehand of the one who wants to believe on Christ Jesus is that he must know and take to heart the way of escape from God’s wrath. The Spirit must convince him of that righteousness. Here a person must understand with some clarity that God has devised a way to save poor lost man by Jesus Christ, whose perfect righteousness has satisfied offended justice and obtained pardon and everlasting favour for all whom He persuades by this gospel to accept God’s offer: “Be it known unto you therefore—that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins; and by him all that believe are justified from all things.” “As many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” So no one is excluded, whatever his rank or condition, and whatever his former way has been, unless he is guilty of the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is a malicious hatred and rejection of the remedy appointed for sinners, as we will hear. For every kind of sin is forgiven to those who accept the offer in God’s way: “He is able to save to the uttermost those that come unto God through him.”

The third thing required beforehand is that a person must know that just as God has not excluded him from the relief appointed, so He is willing to be reconciled to people through Christ, and has bound people to take hold of Him through Christ Jesus and so make that salvation their own. He not only invites all to come (“Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money: come ye, buy and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money, and without price”); He not only welcomes all who come, as we find in the gospel, and commends those who come, like the centurion and the woman of Canaan; He not only rebukes people for not coming and taking hold of Him (“And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life”), and condemns them for not taking hold of Him (“He that believeth not is condemned already”); but He also commands all to believe on Christ: “This is his commandment, that we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ.” So a person is not to question the Lord’s willingness to receive people who go to Christ honestly, for God has made that abundantly clear in Scripture. Unless a person knows this much, he will hardly dare to open his heart to that noble plan of saving sinners, or risk the whole weight of his salvation on Christ Jesus.

The fourth thing required beforehand is that the person who wants to take hold of Christ Jesus must resolve to break all covenants with hell and death: “Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us; for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves.” Whatever known evil people are involved in, they must resolve to give it up, “for there is no concord between Christ and Belial.” The Lord requires that those who expect “him to be for them, should not be for another.” This is far from evangelical repentance, which I grant does not come before a person’s taking hold of Christ by faith. There is little here beyond a disregard for the things a person was formerly devoted to, and a scorn for what he was mad about, because he sees that they have destroyed him and that relief is now offered. At this his heart begins to be more intent than it was before. After this, when Christ is looked at alone, His worth and beauty appear, so that among all the gods there is none like Him, and He appears as a sufficient covering of the eyes to all who get Him. At this the heart loves God’s plan in the new covenant, and loves to lay its weight on Christ rather than on any other way, bending towards Him. And so the person becomes a believer.

Now I will not say that all these things we have spoken of are found formally, in order and distinctly, in every person before he takes hold of God in Christ. For the way of the heart with Christ may be added to “the four wonderful things.” It is difficult to trace the heart in its passage from darkness to light. Yet we set out the most ordinary and likely way for anyone who asks the way. In doing so we bar ignorant and insensible people from meddling with it, and forbid them to claim any interest in Him while they remain like that.

fields.title: The Properties of True Believing
fields.body_html:
IV. THE Fourth thing we proposed to speak of is the properties of this duty when it is rightly carried out. I will mention only a few.

1. Believing on Christ must be personal. A person himself, in his own person, must take hold of Christ Jesus: “The just shall live by his faith.” This means that it is not enough for a person’s safety and relief that he is in covenant with God as a member of the visible church by birth, through his parents’ submission to God’s ordinances. Nor is it enough that he had the initiating seal of baptism added, and that he then in effect pledged himself to seek salvation by Christ’s blood, as all infants do. Nor is it enough that people come from believing parents; their faith will not put their children in possession of a right to the spiritual blessings of the covenant. Nor is it enough that parents in some sense pledged themselves for their children and gave them away to God. None of these things is of any use. The children of the kingdom and of godly ancestors are cast out. Unless a person in his own person puts out faith in Christ Jesus, and with his own heart is pleased with and rests in that plan of saving sinners, he cannot be saved. I grant that this faith is given to him by Christ, but it is certain that it must be personal.

2. This duty must be sincere and heartfelt: “With the heart man believeth unto righteousness.” A person must be sincere and without deceit in taking hold of Christ, judging Him the only covering of the eyes and not hankering after another way. The matter must not just float about in the head or understanding; it must be in the heart. The person must not only be persuaded that Christ is the way, but warmly persuaded of it, loving and liking the thing and delighting in it, so that “it is all a man’s desire,” as David says of the covenant. If a person is to be sincere and warm about anything, surely he must be so here, in this “one thing that is necessary.” It must not be simply a fancy in the head. It must be a matter of the heart, a matter of the soul; indeed, not a matter in the outer court of the affections, but in the very flower of the affections and in the innermost chamber of the soul, where Christ is formed. Shall a person be sincere about anything, and not about this, which contains all his chief interests and his everlasting state? Shall “the Lord be said to rejoice over a man as a bridegroom rejoiceth over his bride,” and to “rest in his love with joy,” and shall the heart of man not go out to meet Him here? The heart or nothing; love or nothing; married love, which goes from heart to heart; the love of betrothal, or nothing: “My son, give me thine heart.” “Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.” I will not say that as soon as they believe, everyone has an overwhelming, felt love that makes them lovesick. But in believing there must be a rational and kindly love, so well grounded and so deeply committed that many waters cannot quench it. “It is strong as death, and jealousy in it burneth as fire.”

3. The third property or quality of believing, as it goes out after Christ, is that it must be rational. By this I mean that the person should move towards God in Christ with knowledge and understanding, taking up God’s plan of saving sinners by Christ as the Scripture holds it out, not imagining for himself a Christ different from the one the gospel speaks of, or a way of relief through Him different from the one the word of God holds out. So we find knowledge joined to the covenant between God and man as a requirement: “And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the Lord; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God.” “And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the Lord.” I also mean here that a person should be calm in spirit, and as it were in cold blood, when he takes hold of Christ Jesus. It should not be in a mere fit of feeling that soon vanishes: “He that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it.” Nor in a disordered state brought on by some outward distress, as the people were: “When he slew them, then they sought him—and proved not steadfast in the covenant.” Nor under the temptation of some outward, temporary interest, as Simon Magus was when he believed. A person must act rationally here, as master of himself, able to some extent to judge the good or evil of the thing as it stands before him.

4. The fourth property is this: just as faith goes out rationally, so it goes out resolutely. The poor distressed people in the gospel threw themselves on Christ most resolutely. This resoluteness of spirit applies to all the difficulties that lie in the way; it forces its way past them. The person whose heart is being laid out for Christ Jesus cannot say, “There is a lion in the street.” If he cannot get in by the door, he will break through the roof of the house, like that man: “And when they could not find by what way they might bring him in because of the multitude, they went upon the house-top, and let him down through the tiling, with his couch, into the midst before Jesus.” He often pays no regard to what the world calls discretion or prudence, like Zacchaeus climbing a tree to see Christ when faith was forming in his breast. This resoluteness of spirit looks ahead to whatever inconveniences may follow and disregards them all, or at least resolves to go on in spite of them all, like a “wise builder, who reckoneth the expense beforehand.” This resoluteness also applies to all a person’s idols and the weights that would easily entangle him if he did not follow Christ over them all, like the blind man who threw off his cloak when Christ called him. This resoluteness in the soul comes from the person’s desperate need within himself, as it was with the jailer; from the sovereign command of God binding the person to move towards Christ, “This is his commandment, that we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ”; and from the good report that has gone out about God, that “he putteth none away that come unto him through Christ,” but commends those who venture over the greatest difficulties, like the woman of Canaan. But above all, this resoluteness comes from the arm of JEHOVAH, secretly and strongly drawing the sinner towards Christ: “No man can come to me, except the Father, which hath sent me, draw him.”

I will not say that everyone who takes hold of Christ in the offers of the gospel has all these thoughts formally in his mind. Yet on searching it will be found that if he is put to it, or reminded of these things, they are then uppermost in the soul.

From what has been said it plainly appears that many in the visible church need to do something more to make their souls secure, when they come to years of discretion, than they are found to have done before in the covenant between God and the church that was sealed to them in baptism.

From what has been said there is also an adequate guard on the free grace of God held out in the gospel through Christ Jesus, so that ignorant, insensible and profane people cannot, with any shadow of reason, claim an interest in it. It is true that believing in Christ and taking hold of Him as a perfect Saviour seems easy, and every godless person says he believes on Him. But they deceive themselves, since their soul has never gone out after Christ Jesus heartily, rationally and resolutely, as we have said. Perhaps some wicked people have been enlightened and have felt some stirring in their fear (Felix trembled) or in their joy (“He that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it,” and “Herod heard John gladly”). But not “having engaged their heart in approaching to God,” they have either settled down in that common work as their sanctuary until the test came (“When tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended”); or “they return back with the dog to their vomit,” from which they had to some extent “escaped, by the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour”; or they fall away completely into hatred and malicious contempt and persecution of Christ and His cause, “from whence hardly can they be recovered”: “For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.” “For if we sin wilfully, after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.—Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?” These things should stir people to be serious in this great business.

We come now to speak of the Fifth thing proposed, the natural consequences of true believing. I will bring what I have to say about them under these two heads: union with God and communion. First, then, I say that when a sinner takes hold of Christ Jesus as has been described, there is at once a wonderful union, a remarkable oneness, between God and the person. Just as husband and wife, head and body, root and branches are not to be counted two but one, so Christ, or God in Christ, and the sinner who takes hold of Him by faith are one: “We are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones,” etc. “He that is so joined unto the Lord, is one spirit.” “As the Father is in the Son, and Christ in the Father; so believers are one in the Father, and the Son: they are one, as the Father and the Son are one. The Father in Christ, and Christ in believers, that they may be made perfect in one.” Oh, what a remarkable interweaving and unbreakable union there is!

Because of this union between God and the believer:

1. They can never hate one another. From now on the Lord will never hate the believer: “As no man hateth his own flesh at any time, but cherisheth and nourisheth it,” so Christ does with His people. He may be angry, so as to correct and discipline the person who is a believer, but everything He does to him is for his good and benefit. “All the Lord’s paths must be mercy and truth to him.” “All things must work together for good to him.” On the other side, the believer can never hate God maliciously, for “he that is born of God sinneth not.” For the Lord has resolved and ordained things in such a way that His hand will undoubtedly be on all believers for good, so that they will never be allowed to hate Him and so be plucked out of His hand.

2. Because of this union there is a remarkable sympathy and fellow feeling between God and the believer. “The Lord is afflicted with the man’s affliction.” He feels it tenderly, carefully and at the right time, as if He were afflicted by it. “He who toucheth the believer, toucheth the apple of the Lord’s eye.” “He is touched with the feeling of their infirmities,” and “precious in his sight is their blood.” In a word, what is done to them is done to Him, and what is not done to them is not done to Him: “He that receiveth you, receiveth me.” “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.—Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.” On the other side, “the zeal of his house” works in the believer’s heart. “The Lord’s reproach” falls on the believer. Whether His affairs go well is the business of His people. So there is a remarkable sympathy between God and believers, all because of the union between them. Because of it, people should hate everything that would compete with Him in their love or affections, and should scorn to be slaves to the creatures, since these are the servants of their Lord and husband, and their servants through Him. What a hateful thing it would be for a queen to have improper dealings with the servants of her prince and husband! It is also a shame for a believer to be “afraid of evil tidings,” since the Lord, with whom he is one, alone rules all things, “and doth whatsoever pleaseth him in heaven and earth.” “All things are yours, and ye are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” “Surely he shall not be moved for ever, he shall not be afraid of evil tidings; his heart is fixed, trusting in the Lord; his heart is established, he shall not be afraid.” “Our God is in the heavens, he hath done whatsoever he pleased.”

The other great consequence of believing is a wonderful, unequalled communion, by virtue of which:

1. The parties themselves belong to each other. The Lord is the God of His people. He Himself, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is their God in all His glorious attributes, His justice as well as His mercy, His wisdom, power, holiness and so on. For He becomes the God of His people, as He often says in the covenant. On the other side, believers are His people. In their very persons they are His, as the covenant says: they shall be His people. Their head, their heart, their hand and so on, whatever they are, they are His.

2. By virtue of this communion they have a mutual interest in each other’s whole goods and property, as far as it can be useful. All the Lord’s word belongs to the believer, threats as well as promises, for their good; all His ways, all His works of every kind, special communications, death, devils, indeed all things, as far as they can be useful: “All things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours, and ye are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” On the other side, everything that belongs to the believer is the Lord’s: inheritance, children, life, wife, reputation and so on are all at His disposal. If any of these can be useful to Him, the believer is to give them up; otherwise he makes that communion false and declares himself, to that extent, unworthy of Christ: “If any man come to me, and hate not his father—yea, and his life also, he cannot be my disciple.”

3. By virtue of this communion there should be much intimacy and familiarity between God and the believer. The Lord may meddle with anything that belongs to the believer and do to him whatever seems good to Him. And the person is not to misjudge Him or say to God, “What dost thou?”, except as far as it concerns his duty. Indeed, he is still to say in every case, “Good is the word and will of the Lord.” On the other side, the believer may, in a humble way, be homely and familiar with God in Christ. He may “come with boldness to the throne of grace,” and need not use a lot of compliments when he speaks to God. For “he is no more a stranger unto God,” so he does not need to speak to God like someone who has to make His acquaintance afresh every hour, as many who profess religion do, which makes a great inconsistency in their religion.

The believer may also open his whole heart to God (“I have poured out my soul before the Lord”), and share all his secrets with Him and all his temptations, without fear of being misjudged. The believer may also inquire into what God is doing, as far as it may concern his own duty, or as far as it may guard against mistakes about the Lord’s way and reconcile it with His words. So Job says, “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him; but I will maintain mine own ways before him.” In this respect the believer is a friend, as “knowing what the Master doth.”

The believer may also be homely with God by going to Him daily with his failings and seeking repentance, pardon and peace through Christ’s advocacy: “Him hath God exalted with his right hand, to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.” “If any man sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” Oh, how often in one day the believer may plead for pardon, as long as he does not intend to mock God or turn grace into licence! The Lord has commanded people to “forgive seventy times seven times in one day,” and has shown there in the parable “of a King who took account of his servants” how much more the Master will forgive.

The believer may also be homely enough to entrust God with all his outward concerns, for He does care about these things: “If God so clothe the grass of the field—shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith? Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed? For your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.” “Casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you.” Indeed, the believer may humbly ask God to come through for him in all such cases, as is fitting, and to help him to bear suitable fruit in every season, “even grace in time of need.” Indeed, how great are the things believers may seek from Him in Christ Jesus, both for themselves and for others! “If we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us.” “Whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do.” “Ask of me things to come concerning my sons; and concerning the work of my hands command ye me.” It is the shame and great loss of His people that they do not make more use of that communion with God than they do. Christ may rightly reproach them “that they ask nothing in his name.”

From what has been said it appears how important this duty of believing is, by which a person takes hold of Christ Jesus, whom the Father has sealed and given as a covenant to the people. It is so honouring to God, answering His very design and serving His purpose in the whole plan and revelation of the gospel, and it is so beneficial to people, that Satan and an evil heart of unbelief oppose it fiercely by raising objections against it. I will point out some of the most common.

fields.title: Objections from Unworthiness and the Heinousness of Sin
fields.body_html:
Objection. I AM so low, so worthless and so weak in myself that I think it would be great presumption for me to have anything to do with Christ Jesus, or with the salvation bought with the price of his blood.

Answer. It is true that all the children of Adam are low and wicked before him, “who chargeth his angels with folly:” “All nations are less than nothing, and vanity before him.” There is such a gulf between God and men that, unless he himself had designed that covenant and freely offered to deal with men in that way, it would have been high treason for men or angels even to imagine that God should humble himself and become a servant; that he should take our nature and unite it in a personal union to the blessed Godhead; and that he should submit himself to the shameful death of the cross; and all this so that men, who were rebels, might be reconciled to God and made eternally happy by being in his holy company for ever.

But I say, all this was his own design and free choice. And more than that, if God had not sovereignly commanded men to close with him in and through Christ, no one would have dared to make use of that design of his: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money: come ye, buy and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.” “And this is his commandment, That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ.” So then, although with Abigail I may say, “Let me be but a servant, to wash the feet of the servants of my lord,” yet he has in his holy wisdom designed that way and knows how to be richly glorified in it: “The eyes of your understanding being enlightened, that ye may know—what is the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.” “All mine are thine, and thine are mine, and I am glorified in them.” And he has commanded me, as I must answer for it on the great day, to close with him in Christ. So, as I have said, I dare not disobey him, nor question the reasons for his plans and commands. I must obey the command, unless I want to be found one who “frustrates the grace of God,” and in a way disappoints the gospel, and falsifies “the record which God hath borne of his Son, that there is life enough in him for men,” and so “makes God a liar,” adding that rebellion to all my earlier sins.

Objection. I am an unusually sinful person, worse than anyone I know; so I dare not presume to come near Christ Jesus, or to seek the salvation that comes through his righteousness.

Answer. Is your sin worse than the drunkenness and incest of Lot; than adultery covered up with murder in David; than idolatry and dreadful apostasy in Solomon; than idolatry, murder and witchcraft in Manasseh; than anger against God and his ways in Jonah; than Peter’s denying Christ with an oath, after he had been warned and had vowed the opposite; than Paul’s bloody persecution, which drove the saints to blaspheme? and so on. But woe to anyone who is made bold to sin by these examples, which are recorded in Scripture and brought forward here to commend the free and rich grace of God and to encourage poor penitent sinners to flee to Christ. I ask, are your sins worse than these? Yet all of these obtained pardon through Christ, as the Scripture shows.

Know, then, that all sins are equal before the free grace of God, “who loveth freely,” and does not look at whether the sin is less or more. If the person has a heart to “come unto him through Christ, then he is able to save to the uttermost.” In fact, it is more provoking to God not to close with Christ when the offer comes to someone than all the rest of his sins are; for “he that believeth not hath made God a liar, in that record he hath borne of life in the Son.” “And he who doth not believe, shall be condemned for not believing on the Son of God.” That will be the main charge against him; so a great deal of sin cannot excuse anyone who rejects Christ and refuses his offer, since God has openly declared that “this is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ came to save sinners, whereof I am chief.” Even the one who is chief of sinners in his own eyes is bound to believe and accept this saying.

Objection. My sins have some aggravating circumstances beyond the same sins in other people, and this terrifies me.

Answer. What aggravations can your sins have that are not matched in the examples above? Was your sin against great light? So, necessarily, were many of those we spoke of. Was it against unusual mercies and deliverances? So was the drunkenness of Lot and of Noah. Was your sin committed with much deliberation? So was David’s, while he wrote the letter against Uriah. Was it against, or after, some unusual revelation of God? So was Solomon’s. Was it through a small and contemptible temptation? So was Jonah’s and Peter’s, if we consider how heinous their sin was. Have you repeated the sin and committed it again? So did Lot, so did Peter, and so did Jehoshaphat in joining with Ahab and Jehoram. Are many gross sins combined in you? So they were in Manasseh. Have you held out long in rebellion? That, like the rest, is your shame; but so did the “thief on the cross;” he held out to the last hour. If even now “thou hast an ear to hear,” you are commanded “to hear.” Although you have long “spent your money for that which is not bread,” you have all the more need now to hurry and flee for refuge; and if you do, he will welcome you and “in nowise cast thee out,” especially since he has set no time limit in Scripture. So none of the aggravations of your sin will excuse you for refusing the Lord’s offer.

Objection. In all these examples you have not named the particular things I am guilty of; nor do I know anyone who ever obtained mercy from God while guilty of such things as are in me.

Answer. It is hard to go into every particular sin that may trouble the conscience; indeed, lesser sins than some I have mentioned may greatly disturb a person if the Lord awakens a sense of guilt. But, to satisfy you, I will go into some truths of Scripture which reach sins and cases more universally than anyone could by listing them one by one: “God pardoneth iniquity, transgression, and sin;” that is, every kind of sin. “If a man turn from all his wickedness, it shall no more be remembered, or prove his ruin.” “Him that cometh, he will in nowise cast out;” that is, whatever his sins are, or their aggravations. “Whosoever believeth shall have everlasting life;” that is, without exception for any sin or any case. “He is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him”—no one can fully declare what God’s uttermost is. “All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men;” that is, there is no kind of sin of which some instance will not be forgiven in one person or another, “except the sin against the Holy Ghost.” These and similar Scriptures sweep every kind of sin before them; so, whatever your sins are or could be, they can be sunk in one of these truths. Your sin, then, can be no excuse for refusing the offer of peace and salvation through Christ, since “any man who will” is allowed to “come and take.”

We will not multiply words. The great God of heaven and earth has sovereignly commanded all who see their need of relief to turn to Christ Jesus and to close wholeheartedly with God’s design for saving sinners by him, laying aside all objections and excuses. They must answer to him for it on the day when he judges the living and the dead, and drives from his presence all who dare to say that their sins and condition were such that they did not dare to venture on Christ’s perfect righteousness for their relief, in spite of the Lord’s own command, given again and again, with his own word, as it were, pledged on it.

fields.title: Of the Sin Against the Holy Ghost
fields.body_html:
Objection. I SUSPECT I am guilty of the “sin against the Holy Ghost,” and so am beyond pardon; and so there is no point in my thinking of believing on Christ Jesus for the saving of my soul.

Answer. No one should charge this sin on themselves or on others unless they can prove the charge and make it plain, following Christ’s example: “And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.” Yet, to settle the doubt, I will: 1. Show what is not the sin against the Holy Ghost, properly so called, because there are some gross sins which people wrongly judge to be this unpardonable sin. 2. Show what the sin against the Holy Ghost is. 3. Draw some conclusions that answer the objection directly.

I. As for the first: there are many gross sins which are not “the sin against the Holy Ghost,” the unpardonable sin, even though, like all other sins, they are sins against the Holy Ghost, who is God, equal and one with the Father and the Son, and are committed against some of his workings and promptings. For example:

1. Blaspheming God under bodily torture is not that sin; for some saints fell into this: “And I punished them oft in every synagogue, and compelled them to blaspheme.” Still less is blaspheming God in a fit of madness or delirium, for a person is not a free, rational agent at such a time; and “he that spareth his people, as a father doth the son that serveth him—and pitieth them that fear him, as a father pitieth his children,” spares and pities them in these wanderings of mind, just as our earthly fathers would if we cursed them in a fit of madness. Still less are horrible blasphemies against God that are shot into the soul, and not welcomed there, this unpardonable sin; for such things were put to Christ, and are often thrown into the minds of the saints.

2. Hating what is good in others while I am not convinced that it is good, but judge it to be evil by the light I have, is not the sin against the Holy Ghost; nor is speaking against it, nor even persecuting it, in that case. All these were found in Paul before he was converted, and he obtained mercy, because he did these things in ignorance.

3. Resentment at the prosperity of others in the work and way of God, while I love the same thing in myself; even resentment against Providence, which often shows itself against the people and things closest to us; even such resentment indulged and kept up, are not that sin, horrible as they are and leading towards that unpardonable sin. These may be found in the saints, coming from a self-love that cannot bear to be overshadowed by another, or from some setback to their idol during a fit of temptation. Most of this was in Jonah.

4. Decline from what was once in a person, and falling into gross sins against light after receiving the truth, are not this unpardonable sin; otherwise many of the saints in Scripture would have been lost. More than that, falling away from much of the truth is not that sin, for it was in Solomon and in the churches of Corinth and Galatia. Even denying, and denying with an oath, the most fundamental truth under a great temptation is not this sin; otherwise Peter would have been lost.

5. Resisting, quenching, grieving and vexing the Spirit of God in many sinful ways are not this unpardonable sin; for they are charged against those who are called to repentance in Scripture, and these people are not shut out as guilty of this sin. In the same way, repeating sin against light is not the sin against the Holy Ghost, although it leads towards it; for such was Peter’s sin in denying Christ, and Jehoshaphat’s sin in joining with Ahab and Jehoram.

6. Intentions and attempts of self-murder, and even intentions of murdering godly people, while the person is in a dark fit of temptation, are not the sin against the Holy Ghost. Even actual self-murder is not, although in its outcome it is probably often joined to this unpardonable sin, and this should make every soul look on the very temptation to it with horror and loathing. The jailer intended to kill himself for a worse reason than many poor people do under the sight and sense of God’s wrath and of their own sin and corruption; yet that jailer obtained pardon. And Paul, before his effectual calling, was an accessory to the murder of many saints, and intended to kill more, as he himself admits: “I verily thought with myself, that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Which thing I also did in Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death, I gave my voice against them. And I punished them oft in every synagogue, and compelled them to blaspheme: and, being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto strange cities.”

All these are dreadful sins, each of them deserving everlasting wrath, and if they are not repented of they bring endless vengeance; the last especially cuts off hope of relief, as far as can be expected in the ordinary way. Yet none of these is the unpardonable sin against the Holy Ghost, and so under any of them there is hope for anyone who has an ear to hear the joyful sound of the covenant. Every kind of such sin and blasphemy may be forgiven, as is plain in the Scriptures where these things are mentioned.

II. As for the second thing, let us see what the sin against the Holy Ghost is. It is not a single act of sin, but a combination of many evil things, usually involving soul and body in guilt. We describe it like this: “It is a rejecting and opposing of the chief gospel truth and way of salvation, which the Spirit of God has made plain to a person in particular, both in its truth and in its goodness; and that openly, freely, wilfully, maliciously and spitefully, producing hopeless fear.” There are three passages of Scripture which speak most of this sin, and from them we will prove every part of this description, as far as is useful for our present purpose. From this it will be clear that no one who has a desire for Christ needs to stumble at what Scripture says about this sin: “Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men. And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.”—“For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.”—“For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries. He that despised Moses’ law died without mercy under two or three witnesses; of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?”

1. First, let us consider the object that this sin, the sinful action of the person guilty of it, is concerned with: the chief gospel truth and way of salvation, which come to one and the same thing. It is the way God has designed for saving sinners by Jesus Christ, the promised Messiah and Saviour, by whose death and righteousness people are to be saved, as he has held him out in the ordinances and confirmed it by many mighty works recorded in Scripture. This way of salvation is the object. The Pharisees opposed this, that Christ was the Messiah: “And all the people said, Is not this the Son of David? But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils.” The wrong is done against the Son of God: “It is impossible to renew them again unto repentance, seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame;” and against the blood of the covenant, and against the Spirit graciously offering to apply these things: “Of how much sorer punishment suppose ye shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?”

2. In the description, consider what is true of this object: it is made plain to the person in a particular way by the Spirit of God, both in its truth and in its goodness. This means, first, that there must be knowledge of the truth and way of salvation. The Pharisees knew that Christ was the heir: “But when they saw the Son, they said among themselves, This is the heir, come, let us kill him.” The person has knowledge: “But if we sin wilfully, after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.” Second, that knowledge of the thing must not just float in the head; there must be some half-hearted persuasion of it. “Christ knew the Pharisees’ thoughts,” and so judged them, and judged that the opposite of what they said had been made plain to their hearts. There is a tasting which goes beyond mere enlightening: “For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and have tasted of the good word of God, and of the powers of the world to come.” Indeed, there is usually a persuasion that leads to a good deal of outward holiness: “Who hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith they were sanctified, an unholy thing.” Third, this persuasion must be not only of the truth of the thing but of its goodness: the person “tasteth the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come,” and sees the thing as worth choosing. Fourth, this persuasion is produced not only by force of argument but also by an enlightening work of God’s Spirit, shining on the truth and making it plain to see; that is why this sin is called “the sin against the Holy Ghost.” The people are said to have been “made partakers of the Holy Ghost,” and to “do despite unto the Spirit of grace,” who was within a step of a saving work in them.

3. In this description, consider what the person does against the object so described: he rejects and opposes it. This means, first, that people have at one time, in some way at least, had dealings with it, or had it offered to them, as was true of the Pharisees. Second, that they reject, even with contempt, what they had of it or had offered to them. The Pharisees deny it and speak scornfully of Christ: “This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils.” They “fall away,” intending to “put Christ to an open shame.” Third, these people set themselves against it in a spirit of persecution, as the Pharisees always did. They rail against it; that is why it is called “blasphemy against the Holy Ghost.” They would “crucify Christ again” if they could. They are adversaries.

4. Consider the marks of this action. First, it is open; that is, it does not try to shelter or hide itself. The Pharisees speak against Christ publicly: “But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub, the prince of the devils.” They want “Christ brought to an open shame.” They abandon the ordinances that carry the flavour of that way: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is;” and they despise the danger, for while “looking for indignation,” they still trample on that blood. Second, the person acts freely. It is not from thoughtlessness, nor from force or compulsion, but an act of free choice. Nothing forced the Pharisees to speak against and persecute Christ. They “crucify to themselves;” they repeat the murder of their own free will and in their own hearts, with no one forcing them. They sin by free choice, or, as the word may be translated, spontaneously: “For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.” Third, it is done wilfully. They are so determined that they will not be turned from it by any offer or by the most precious means, as is clear in the Scriptures above. Fourth, it is done maliciously, so that it comes little, if at all, from a temptation to pleasure, profit or honour. It does not come from fear, or force, or from any good aim, but from malice of heart against God and Christ and the advance of his glory and kingdom. So it is of the very nature of Satan’s sin, who has an irreconcilable hatred against God and against the remedy for sin, because God’s glory is advanced by it. This is a special ingredient in this sin. The Pharisees are found guilty of malice of heart against Christ, since they spoke this way against him and not against their own children casting out devils; and this is the force of Christ’s argument: “If I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your children cast them out?” They do their utmost “to crucify Christ again, and to bring him to an open shame.” They are adversaries, like the devil. Fifth, it is done spitefully; the malice must show itself. The Pharisees must proclaim that Christ is in league with devils; he must be “put to an open shame, and crucified again;” they must “tread under foot that blood, and do despite to the Spirit.” So the person would rather perish a thousand times than be in Christ’s debt for salvation.

5. The last thing in the description is what usually accompanies or follows this sin: it produces desperate and hopeless fear. They fear the one they hate with a slavish, hopeless fear, such as devils have: “A certain fearful looking for of judgment, and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.” They know that God will exert his power against them; they tremble at the thought of it; and if they could get above him and destroy him, they would. Since they cannot do that, they hate him with all the malice of their hearts, and persecute him and all that is his with spite.

III. As for the third thing proposed, the conclusions to be drawn from what has been said, by which we will speak directly to the objection. 1. As I hinted before, since the sin against the Holy Ghost is so striking and can be well recognised where it exists, no one should charge themselves with it unless they can prove the charge and make it plain. For it is a great wrong to God to try to persuade my soul that he will never pardon me: it is the very way to drive me to despair and lead me to the unpardonable sin. So, unless you can and dare say that you hate the way God has designed for saving sinners, and are determined to oppose the prosperity of his kingdom, both in yourself and in others, out of malice and spite against God, you ought not to suspect yourself guilty of this sin. 2. Whatever you have done against God, if you repent of it and wish it were undone, you cannot be guilty of this sin; for in it malice of heart and spite against God always prevail. 3. If you are content to be his debtor for pardon, and would be infinitely obliged to him for it, then you cannot in that case be guilty of the sin against the Holy Ghost; for, as we showed before, those who are guilty of it so despise God that they would not be his debtors for salvation. 4. Whatever you have done, if you have a desire for Jesus Christ, and look after him with a grieved heart, and cannot bear the thought of parting from his blessed company for ever; or, if you must part with him, still wish him and all who are his well, you need not suspect yourself guilty of this unpardonable sin; for there can be no such hatred of him in your heart as that sin necessarily requires. 5. If you want to be beyond the reach of that sin and safe from it for ever, then go and work your heart up to be pleased with salvation by Christ Jesus, and to close with God in him, resting content in him as the sufficient ransom and rest, as we have been urging before, and yield to him to be saved in his way. Do this in good earnest, and you will be for ever out of the reach of that deadly thing with which Satan frightens so many poor seekers of God.

fields.title: Objections from Want of Power and Unfruitfulness
fields.body_html:
Objection. EVEN if I am not shut out from the benefit of the new covenant, it is still not in my power to believe on Christ; for faith is the gift of God, and beyond the strength of flesh and blood.

Answer. It is true that saving faith, by which alone a person can wholeheartedly close with God in Christ, is beyond our power and is the gift of God, as we said earlier. Yet remember: 1. The Lord has laid it as a duty on all who hear this gospel to close wholeheartedly, by faith, with his offer of salvation through Christ, as is clear in Scripture. And you must know that, although it is not in our own power to perform that duty, the Lord may justly condemn us for not performing it, and we are without excuse; because at the beginning he made man perfectly able to do whatever he should command. 2. In commanding this thing which is beyond our power, the Lord wants us to feel our inability to do it, and wants us to look to him to work it in us. He has promised to give the new heart, and he has not shut anyone out from the benefit of that promise. 3. The Lord’s way is to use these commands and invitations, and people’s meditation on them and their prayers about the matter, to give the soul power to perform the duty.

So, in answer to the objection, I beg you, in the Lord’s name, to take these commands and promises of his to heart, and to meditate on them and on that blessed business of the new covenant. Pray to God over them as well as you can, “for he will be inquired to do these things.” Bring your cold heart to God’s design as it is set out in Scripture, and to Christ Jesus, who is given for a covenant to the people, and look to him for life and quickening. Go and try to be pleased with that salvation in the way God offers it, and to close with and rest on Christ for it, as if it were all in your power; and yet look to him for it, knowing that it must come from him. If you do this, “he who meets those who remember him in his ways” will not fail on his part, and you will have no grounds to say that you moved towards the thing until you could do no more for lack of strength, and so left it at God’s door. It will not fail on his side if you have a heart for the business. In fact, I may say that if, from all you have ever heard of this matter, your heart loves it and wants to be committed to it, you have already done it within yourself, and that difficulty is past before you were aware of it.

Objection. Many who have closed with Christ Jesus, as has been described, still complain of their leanness and fruitlessness, and this makes my heart put less weight on that duty of believing.

Answer. If you are convinced that it is a duty to believe on Christ, as has been described, you must not refuse it on any pretext. As for the complaints of some who have sought after him, without allowing everyone to be the judge of his own fruit, I say:

1. Many, by their suspicions of God’s love and by their unbelief after they have closed with God in this way, block many precious gifts which would otherwise be given to them: “And he did not many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.”

2. It cannot be that anyone whose heart has gone out after Christ “has found him a wilderness.” Surely they find something in their spirit drawing them towards God in these two great things. First, how to be found in him on that day: “Yea, doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord; for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung that I may win Christ, and be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith.” Second, how to live to his praise in the land of the living: “Deal bountifully with thy servant, that I may live and keep thy word:” “Wilt thou not deliver my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the land of the living?” They find these two things uppermost in the soul, and that is a great deal. Moreover, if they search and judge rightly, they will always find an emptiness in created things which an abundance of them cannot fill. All is vanity; only God can fill the empty room in their heart, and when he breathes on it even a little, there is no room for any further comfort from created things. This shows that God has captured the person and has fixed that saving principle in the understanding and the heart. “Who is God but the Lord? worship him all ye gods.” Further still, those whose hearts have closed with God in Christ, as has been described, will not deny that now and then, when the soul was about to fail, there have been timely mercies that came before them and timely quickenings: “For thou preventest me with the blessings of thy goodness.” “When I said, My foot slippeth, thy mercy, O Lord, held me up. In the multitude of my thoughts within me, thy comforts delight my soul.” So let no one say that no fruit follows, and let no one neglect their duty because of the unjust and groundless complaints of others.

fields.title: Of Covenanting with God
fields.body_html:
Objection. ALTHOUGH I judge it my duty to close with God’s design in the covenant, I am in the dark about how to go about that duty. For sometimes God offers to be our God without any mention of Christ, and sometimes says that he will betroth us to himself; and in other places of Scripture we are called to come to Christ, and he is the Bridegroom. Again, God sometimes speaks of himself as a Father to people, sometimes as a Husband; Christ is sometimes called the Husband and sometimes a Brother. These relationships seem inconsistent, and leave me very much in the dark about how to think of God when my heart wants to agree with him and close with him.

Answer. It may very well be said that people come to God, or close with him, and yet that they come to Christ and close with him. They may be said to come into a marriage relationship with God, and with Christ also, who is husband, father, brother and so on to them; and there is no such mystery here as some imagine.

To understand it better, consider these few things.

1. Although God made man perfect at the beginning, and gave him some capacity to deal with him directly—“God hath made man upright:” “And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat,” and so on—yet by his fall man put himself at such a distance from God that he became utterly unable to bargain or deal with him directly any more.

2. After Adam’s fall the Lord revealed the new covenant, in which he showed that he was willing to deal with man again, in and through a Mediator. So he appointed people to come to him through Christ: “He is able to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him;” and to look for acceptance only in him: “To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the Beloved.” He ordained that people should listen to Christ, since he was the only one in whom God was well pleased: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, hear ye him.”

3. This matter is so clear, and is taken to be so prominent in Scripture and so plain to all who sit under the ordinances, that the Lord often speaks of dealing with himself without mentioning the Mediator, because it is assumed that everyone in the church knows that there is now no dealing with God except by and through Christ Jesus the Mediator.

4. Consider that Christ Jesus, God and man, is not only a fit place for God and men to meet, and a fit mediator to negotiate between the parties now at odds: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself;” but we may also say that he is himself the bridegroom. So our closing or dealing with God may rightly be called the marriage of the King’s son, and the elect may be called the Lamb’s wife; Christ Jesus being, as it were, the hand which God holds out to people, and which they take hold of when they deal with God. And so through and by Christ we close with God as our God, in whom our soul finally and ultimately comes to rest through Christ: “Who by him do believe in God that raised him from the dead, and gave him glory, that your faith and hope might be in God.”

5. Consider that the various relationships mentioned in Scripture are given to show the sure and unbreakable union and communion between God and his people. Whatever bond there is between head and members, root and branches, king and subjects, shepherd and flock, father and children, brother and brother, husband and wife and so on, it is all here: “And they all shall be one, as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one: I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, as thou hast loved me. And I have declared unto them thy name, and will declare it; that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them.” So, whatever Scripture says, people may be sure that God is calling them to be reconciled to him through Christ, and is offering himself to be their God and husband in him alone. And people are to accept God as their God in Christ, being pleased with that way of relief for poor man, and to give themselves up to God in Christ, in whom alone they can be accepted. Those who close with Christ close with God, who is in Christ “reconciling the world to himself.” And we are not to delve further into the various relationships between God or Christ and people mentioned in Scripture than as they point to union and communion, or nearness to God through Christ Jesus, and to our benefit from it.

Since these things are clear, we will not multiply words. But since believing on Christ is the great duty required of all who hear this gospel, we beg everyone to whom the knowledge of this comes, in the Lord’s name, to take to heart without delay their lost condition in themselves. Let them take to heart the remedy God has provided by Jesus Christ, which he has freely offered to all who will be content with it and willing to be saved that way. Let them take to heart that there is no other way of escape from the wrath to come; to escape it, people would gladly, on the last day, run into a lake of molten lead to be hidden from the face of the Lamb whom they despise here. We say, we beg all people, as they consider these things, to work their hearts up to this business, to open themselves to God, and to receive him through Christ in the offers of the gospel, resting content in him as the only desirable and satisfying good, so that they may make themselves safe. Go quickly and search for his offers of peace and salvation in Scripture, and work your heart and soul up to close with them, and with Christ in them, and with God in Christ. Do it in such a way that you can say you were as serious, earnest and wholehearted in this as you have ever been in anything, as far as you can tell; and that, as far as you know, Christ is the choice of your heart, or at least that you neither know of nor allow anything to the contrary. On that basis your heart appeals to God to search and test whether anything is wrong, to put it right, and to lead you into the right way.

Now, this cleaving of the heart to him, and throwing itself on him to be saved in his way, is believing. It does indeed make a person safe from the wrath to come, because he has now received Christ and believes on him, and so shall not come into condemnation, as the Scripture says.

Objection. When I hear what it is to believe on Christ Jesus, I sometimes think I have faith; for I dare say that, as far as I can tell, I am pleased with the method of saving sinners by Christ Jesus; my heart goes out after him and rests on him as a satisfying treasure; and I am glad to accept God to be my God in him. But I often question whether I have ever done so, and so am kept, most of the time, hesitating and doubting whether I believe, or am savingly in covenant with God.

Answer. It is common for many whose hearts have gone out after Christ in the gospel, and who have received him, to call the same thing into question again. So I will recommend one thing as a remarkable help for fixing the soul in keeping hold of faith and of an interest in God. It is that people should not only close wholeheartedly with God in Christ, as has been described, but should also “expressly, explicitly, by word of mouth, and viva voce, formally close with Christ Jesus, and accept God’s offer of salvation through him, and so make a covenant with God.” By God’s blessing this may do no small amount to settle them about their saving interest in God.

Before I speak directly of this “express covenanting with God,” I set down these few things first:

1. I do not mean here a covenanting with God that differs in essence from the covenant between God and the visible church as the Lord holds it out in his revealed will; nor do I mean a covenant that differs in essence from the dealing of the heart with God in Christ spoken of earlier. It is the same covenant; it differs only in one particular circumstance, namely, the formal expression of what the heart had already done.

2. I grant that this express covenanting and dealing with God is not absolutely necessary for a person’s salvation. If anyone closes wholeheartedly and sincerely with God offering himself in Christ in the gospel, his soul and state are made safe by it, according to Scripture, even if he says no words with his mouth. But this express, spoken covenanting with God is very helpful for the well-being of a person’s state, and for keeping hold of an interest in Christ Jesus with more comfort.

3. This express covenanting with God by word of mouth is worth nothing unless it is joined with a sincere closing of the heart with God in Christ. Without that, it is only a profaning of the Lord’s name and a mocking of him to his face, “to draw near to him with the lips, whilst the heart is far away from him.”

4. I grant that neither the heart’s dealing with God nor the spoken dealing will make a person’s state of grace plain to him, so as to put and keep it beyond dispute, without the joint witness of the Spirit, by which we know the things that are freely given to us by God.
