Yet this explicit way of dealing with God, joined with the heart’s closing with him in Christ, does much to make it clear to a person that there is a settled bargain between God and him. It will do much to fend off many groundless suspicions and objections of an unstable mind and heart, which shamefully tends to deny this hour what it really did and performed the hour before. This explicit covenanting is like a formal record of what passed between God and the soul, and so it has its own advantage for strengthening faith.

As for this express covenanting, we will: 1. Show that it is a fully warranted practice. 2. Show briefly what preparation is required of those who deal with God in this way. 3. Show how people should go about that duty. 4. Show what should follow from it.

I. As to the first, I say that it is a warranted practice, and a binding duty, to covenant with God expressly and in words. This appears as follows.

1. In many places of Scripture, if we look at what they can bear according to their scope and the analogy of faith, God has commanded it and laid it on people as a duty: “One shall say, I am the Lord’s.” “Surely, shall one say, In the Lord have I righteousness and strength.” “Wilt thou not from this time cry unto me, My Father, thou art the guide of my youth.” “They shall say, The Lord is my God.” “Thou shalt call me Ishi;” and in many other places. Now, since God has so clearly laid it on people in the letter of the word, they may be persuaded that it is a practice he warrants and allows, and one that pleases him well.

2. It is the approved practice of the saints in Scripture to covenant with God expressly in this way, and they found much comfort in that duty afterwards. David often said expressly to God that he was his God and his portion, and that he himself was his servant. Thomas puts his interest beyond question with it: “And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord, and my God.” Indeed, I say, the saints are greatly comforted in remembering what has passed in this way between God and them: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee.” “I cried unto thee, O Lord, I said, Thou art my refuge, and my portion in the land of the living.” We often find it so in the Song of Songs. Now, shall God’s chief worthies be so much given to a duty which gives them so much peace and satisfaction in many situations, and shall we, under the New Testament, to whom access is so abundantly given and who share in the sap of the olive tree, shall we, I say, fall behind in this approved work of communion with God? Since we try to imitate that cloud of witnesses in other things, such as faith, zeal and patience, let us imitate them in this too.

3. The thing we are speaking about here is the matter of greatest concern in all the world: “It is the life of our soul.” Oh! Will people take care to be express, explicit, plain and definite in all their other important business, because it is important, and will they not be much more definite and express in this, which concerns them most? I wonder that many not only fail to speak it with their mouths, but do not swear it and sign it with their hands, and do everything the Scriptures warrant to secure God to themselves in Christ, and themselves to God: “One shall say, I am the Lord’s; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the Lord, and surname himself by the name of Israel.”

This also may carry weight as an argument for urging this way of covenanting with God: in the experience of the saints, the matter of an interest in Christ, and of real and honest dealing with him, is the thing most often brought into debate and called into question. So people need every means they can find, in thought, word and deed, to settle it.

This also may be urged here to press it as a duty: God is so formal, express, precise and, so to speak, legal in the whole business of man’s salvation. Christ must be a near kinsman, to whom the right of redemption belongs; he must be chosen, called, authorised and sent; covenants are formally drawn up between the Father and him, the Father accepts payment and satisfaction and gives formal discharges, and all is done clearly and expressly. Shall the Lord be so express, plain and definite in every part of the business, and shall our part of it rest in a confused thought, while we stand like dumb beasts before him? In a marriage between man and wife, it would not be thought enough that the woman consented in her heart and the man knew it, if she never said so in words when she was able to. Now, this covenant between God and man is presented in Scripture as a marriage between man and wife: “And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness and in judgment, and in loving-kindness and in mercies: I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness; and thou shalt know the Lord.”—“For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The whole Song of Solomon speaks of it. The Lord uses comparisons to show us what he means; and surely this is one particular requirement in marriage, that the wife gives express and explicit consent to it. The man says, “So I take thee to be my lawful wife, and do oblige myself to be a dutiful husband.” The woman for her part is bound to express her consent and say, “Even so I take thee to be my lawful husband, and do promise duty and subjection.” It is the same here. The Lord says, “I do betroth thee unto me in faithfulness, and thou shalt call me Ishi,” that is, my husband. I will be a head and husband to you, if “thou wilt not be for another.” The person ought to answer and say, Amen, so be it; you shall be my God, my Head and Lord, and I shall and will be yours, and not another’s: “I am my Beloved’s, and my Beloved is mine.” And so this making of the covenant with God is called “a giving of the hand to him,” as the word is: “Now, be ye not stiff-necked, as your fathers were, but yield yourselves unto the Lord, and enter into his sanctuary, which he hath sanctified for ever; and serve the Lord your God, that the fierceness of his wrath may turn away from you.” This implies a very express, formal, explicit and definite bargaining with God. So we conclude that it is a binding duty and a well-approved practice, needed for quieting a person’s mind and for his being in covenant with God with more comfort, and for answering more fully God’s condescension and offer in that great and primary promise, “I will be your God, and ye shall be my people.”

Not only may and should people deal expressly with God in Christ like this, to fix their hearts; they may also on certain occasions renew this spoken transaction with God, especially when, through temptations, they are made to question whether they have ever really and sincerely entered into covenant with God. Just as they are then to exercise new acts of faith, embracing Christ as their desirable portion and treasure, as on other occasions too, so it would be wise, especially if any doubt remains about the matter, to settle that dispute viva voce and in express words, and to “say of the Lord, and to him, that he is their refuge and portion.” We find the saints doing this, and we may imitate them. Especially:

1st, In times of great backsliding, people used to renew the covenant with God, and we should do so too. Our hearts should go out after Christ in the promises of reconciliation with God, for he is our peace when we need it, and our Advocate, and we are bound to look on him that way when we sin: “If any man sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous;” and to express as much in words, as the saints did in their formal renewing of the covenant.

2d, When people are in danger, and difficulties are present or foreseen, it would be good for them to send their hearts out after him and to express their holding fast to him, to make their own hearts secure. We find Joshua doing this when Israel was to settle in the land of Canaan in the midst of snares: “Now therefore fear the Lord, and serve him in sincerity and in truth: and put away the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood, and in Egypt; and serve ye the Lord. And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served, that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. And the people answered and said, God forbid that we should forsake the Lord, to serve other gods; for the Lord our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed: and the Lord drave out from before us all the people, even the Amorites which dwelt in the land: therefore will we also serve the Lord; for he is our God. And Joshua said unto the people, Ye cannot serve the Lord: for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins. If ye forsake the Lord, and serve strange gods, then he will turn and do you hurt, and consume you, after that he hath done you good. And the people said unto Joshua, Nay; but we will serve the Lord. And Joshua said unto the people, Ye are witnesses against yourselves, that ye have chosen you the Lord, to serve him. And they said, We are witnesses. Now therefore put away (said he) the strange gods which are among you, and incline your heart unto the Lord God of Israel. And the people said unto Joshua, The Lord our God will we serve, and his voice will we obey. So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem.” So David does in his troubles: “In the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be over-past.”

3. When people feel that God is far from them, and that their soul is withering and declining, then it is safest to close wholeheartedly with Christ and embrace him by faith to make the soul secure; and it would be good to put it beyond question by saying it. This is the quickest way to draw sap from Christ the root for the recovery of the soul and for establishing the heart before him. The bride in the Song of Solomon does this, asserting her interest in him when she is in that condition, professing and declaring him to be her beloved.

4. At the celebration of the Lord’s Supper, people should close wholeheartedly with God in Christ in this way, and say and express as much; for that is a feast of love, and then and there we come under a solemn profession of closing with God in Christ, personally and openly, and receive the seal of it. So it is fitting at that time to bring both heart and tongue to back up and answer our profession, seeing ourselves as God’s and at his disposal.

We will not tie the Lord’s people to times and seasons for this duty; the Lord may lay it on them as he pleases. Only there is a danger that by covenanting expressly with God too often, people become too formal in it. So it is not so fitting for people regularly to renew that explicit transaction with God at full length. Rather, they should declare to God that they hold to the covenant they made with him, that they stand by it, and will never revoke or withdraw it. With that, they may touch on the sum of it by laying claim to God in Christ as their own God; and this they may do often, even in all their approaches to God. This is probably what the saints meant in their very common practice in Scripture of asserting their interest in God as their God and portion. And it is fitting that people, in all their life, keep their hearts to this business by cleaving to God in Christ. “The life we live in the flesh should be by faith in the Son of God.”

II. As to the second thing, namely, what preparation is required of the one who is to deal with God expressly in this way. Besides what we mentioned before as coming before a person’s closing with Christ Jesus, we only add: 1. Whoever wants to bargain explicitly with God must know that doing so is warranted and allowed by God, as we showed above. If this is missing, a person cannot do it in faith, and so it will be sin to him: “Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.” 2. The person must work to bring his heart up to the thing, so that it does not give the lie to the tongue. It would be a great mockery of God to “draw near him with the lips, whilst the heart is far off from him.”

III. The third thing to be considered in this express spoken covenanting with God is how it is to be done and carried out. Besides what was said before about the heart’s closing with Christ, I add here:

1. The person should do it confidently, not only believing that he is doing his duty when he does it, but also that God in Christ Jesus will accept his poor, imperfect way of doing it. He “accepts a man according to what he hath, if there be a willing mind.” A mite is accepted, since it is “all the poor woman’s substance.” Indeed, if it can be reached, the person should believe that the outcome and result of this transaction will prove comforting and that all will be well; and that God, who undertakes for everything in the covenant, will, since he has brought the person to this happy choice, in some measure make him able to keep it and will perfect what concerns him: “Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it.” If this confidence is missing, the thing will be done with much fear and suspicion, if not worse, and will remain a disturbing business to the person.

2. It should be done with holiness. It is called “the holy covenant,” “the holy things of David.” It would be fitting here that what is done in this express dealing with God should not be done in passing, as an aside, but in a special approach to God; the thing should be spoken to the Lord: “I cried unto thee, O Lord; I said, Thou art my refuge and my portion.” In so great a business it is fitting that some time be set apart for confession and prayer before God. The person dealing with God in this way should also work to have high thoughts of God’s greatness and sovereignty: “Thou art great, O Lord God; for there is none like thee, neither is there any god beside thee,” even though he humbles himself to look on things in heaven and on earth. These high and holy thoughts of him will and should go along with lowly and humbling thoughts of oneself, even while being admitted to this high dignity: “Then went King David in, and sat before the Lord; and he said, Who am I, O Lord God? and what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto?” It is no small thing to be joined to the great God of heaven and his Son Christ, as David said when King Saul offered him his daughter: “Seemeth it to you a light thing to be a king’s son-in-law, seeing that I am a poor man, and lightly esteemed?” Further, there should be special guarding and watching so that the heart stays spiritual in dealing with God. There is great reason for doing the duty in this holy way, for people are apt to deceive themselves, to think of the Lord according to their own imagination, and to become carnal in the business, since it is a marriage transaction set out in all the ordinary language of love, as in the Song of Solomon.

IV. The fourth thing we will speak of is what should follow from this express spoken covenanting with God. I say that, besides the union and communion with God in Christ that follows from believing, if a person deals explicitly with God in words:

1. From then on he should be especially careful to keep close to God in every part of his conduct. For if a person afterwards does anything unfitting, he falsifies his word before God, which will badly wound his conscience and prove a snare. If a person afterwards forsakes God and takes it on himself to dispose of himself, when he is not his own and has opened his mouth to the Lord, “he makes inquiry after vows, and devoureth that which is holy.”

2. The one who deals with God in this way should hold firmly to that decision and conclusion. It is a shame for someone whose heart has closed with God, and whose mouth has solemnly ratified and confirmed it before him, to contradict himself again and to allow anything to the contrary. He ought to stand by it boldly against all opposition.

So let me beg you who want to be settled in the matter of your interest in God: as soon as you conveniently can, set apart some time for prayer before God, and, working to bring your heart up to seriousness, affection and faith in the duty, make a covenant and deal with God in express words, in this way:

“O Lord, I am a lost and fallen creature, by nature and by countless actual sins, which I confess one by one before you today. And although, being born within the visible church, I was in covenant with you from the womb and had that covenant sealed to me in baptism, yet for a long time I have lived without God in the world, unaware of and ignorant of what I owed by virtue of that covenant. At last you have shown me and pressed on my heart my miserable state in myself, and have made plain to my heart the satisfying remedy you have provided by Christ Jesus. You offer it freely to me, on condition that I accept it and close with you as my God in Christ, and you warrant and command me, at my utmost peril, to accept this offer and flee to Christ Jesus. Indeed, as far as I can tell, you have now sovereignly settled my heart and shaped it for Christ Jesus, leading it out after him in the offers of the gospel, causing me to come to the living God, to close with him in this way and to rest content in his offer, without any guile that I know of. And so that I may come to that settledness of spirit in this matter which should be for my comfort and the praise of your glorious grace, I am here today to put the matter beyond question by express words before you, according to your will. And now I, unworthy as I am, declare that I believe that Christ Jesus, who was slain at Jerusalem, was the Son of God and the Saviour of the world. I believe that record, that there is eternal life for people in him, and in him only. Today in my heart I declare myself pleased with, and content to rest in, that method of saving sinners by him, and I entrust my soul to him. I accept reconciliation with God through him, and I close with you as my God in him. I choose him in all that he is and all that may come with him, and I give up myself, and all that I am or have, to you, wanting to be divorced from everything hateful to you, without exception or reservation, or anything inconsistent with this that I know of, or any intended going back. Here I give you my hand, and I take everything around me as witnesses that I, whatever I am or have been until now, accept God’s offer of peace through Christ, and make a sure covenant with you today, never to be reversed. I hope that you will make all things good, both on your part and on mine, and I earnestly beg, as I want to be saved, that my corruptions may be subdued, my neck brought under your sweet yoke in all things, and my heart made to rest cheerfully in whatever you do to me or with me for these ends. Now, glory be to you, O Father, who designed such a salvation and gave the Son to accomplish it. Glory be to Christ Jesus, who at so high a price bought the pouring out of that love from the Father’s heart, through whom alone this access is granted, and in whom I am reconciled to God and honourably united to him, and am no longer an enemy or a stranger. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who alarmed me when I was destroying myself, and who not only convinced me of my danger but also opened my eyes to see the remedy provided in Christ; who persuaded and moved my wicked heart to fall in love with Christ as the treasure that makes rich; and who today teaches me how to covenant with God, how to take to myself all the sure mercies of David and the blessings of Abraham, and how to secure to myself the favour and friendship of God for ever. Now, with my soul, heart, head and whole self, as far as I can, I rest content in the choice I have made today, resolving from now on not to be my own but yours, and that the care of whatever concerns me will be on you, as my Head and Lord. I humbly declare that failings on my part (which you know I resolve against) will not make this covenant void; for so you have said, and I do not intend to abuse it, but all the more to cleave close to you. And I must be free to renew, ratify and draw copies of this transaction as often as is needed. Now, I know that your consent to this bargain stands recorded in Scripture, so that I need no new sign of it; and having accepted your offer on your own terms, I will from now on wait for what is good, and for your salvation in the end. As you are faithful, pardon what is wrong in my way of doing this, and accept me in my sweet Lord Jesus, in whom alone I seek pardon. And as testimony to this, I set my seal that God is true, declaring him a sufficient Saviour.”

Let people covenant with God in fewer or more words, as the Lord leads them; we do not mean to set a form of words for anyone. Only it would be proper for people to acknowledge before the Lord their lost state in themselves and the relief there is by Christ, and to declare that they accept it as it is offered in the gospel, and rest thankfully satisfied with it, entrusting themselves wholly to God from then on, to be saved his way, which they wait for according to his faithfulness.

If people would do this wholeheartedly and sincerely, it might, by the Lord’s blessing, help to settle them against many fears and suspicions. They might date some good thing from that day and hour, which might prove a comfort to them when they fall into darkness afterwards, and even when many failings stare them in the face, perhaps at the hour of death: “These be the last words of David—Although my house be not so with God; yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure; for this is all my salvation; and all my desire.” It is a great thing if a person can appeal to God and say, You know there was a day and an hour when, in such a place, I accepted peace through Christ and gave up my heart to you, for you to write your whole law on it without exception; heaven and earth are witnesses of it. “Remember the word unto thy servant upon which thou hast caused me to hope.”

Objection. I dare not venture to say such words to God, because I do not find my heart rising fully to them in affection and seriousness; so I would only be lying to God in dealing with him like this.

Answer. It is sad that the human heart does not embrace and welcome that blessed offer and portion with great intensity of desire and affection. Yet, in answer to the objection, remember: 1. In those to whom the Lord gives the new heart, forming Christ in them, the whole heart is not yet renewed. There is “flesh and spirit lusting against each other, the one contrary to the other, so that a man can neither do the good or evil he would do” with full strength. It is well if a good part of the heart goes out after Christ, wanting to close with him on his own terms.

2. There is often a reasoned love for Christ Jesus in the heart, which shows itself by regard for his commandments: “This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not grievous.” Even when there is not a strongly felt love that makes the soul sick—“I am sick of love”—people must not always expect to find this. So I say: although something in your heart holds back, if you can say that you are convinced of your lost state without him, that you lack a righteousness to cover your guilt and lack strength to stand out against sin or to do what pleases God, and that you also see fullness in him in both these respects; if you dare say that something within your heart anxiously desires him on his own terms, and would have both righteousness for justification and strength for sanctification; and that whatever in you contradicts this is, in some measure, your burden and your bondage: if that is so, your heart has been brought up a fair way. Go on with the business and settle the matter by covenanting with God, and say with your mouth, “That you have both righteousness and strength in the Lord,” as he has sworn you shall: “I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear. Surely, shall one say, In the Lord have I righteousness and strength: even to him shall men come; and all that are incensed against him shall be ashamed.” It is in keeping with Scripture to say to God, I believe, when there is much unbelief in me and my heart is divided about it: “Lord, I believe, help thou mine unbelief.” At the same time, tell God how things are in your heart, so that you may be without guile before him, hiding nothing from him; and put your heart, as it is, into his hand for him to write his law on it, according to the covenant. For that is what he seeks from people: that they give up their heart to him so that he may stamp it with his whole will, without exception. And if you can wholeheartedly consent to that, judging Christ’s blood a sufficient ransom and satisfaction for human sin, you may go and expressly strike a covenant with God, for your heart and affection are already committed.

Objection. I dare not covenant with God in this way, in case I break with him. In fact, I am convinced that if such a temptation came, in such and such circumstances, I would fall before it and give in. So to deal with God in this way while I foresee such a thing would only make my condemnation worse.

Answer. 1. You have already entered into covenant with God, as a member of his visible church; and what is now urged on you is that you covenant and close with him more wholeheartedly, sincerely, personally and expressly. You are already bound to close wholeheartedly with God in Christ, and if you do it in your heart, I hope the danger is no greater for saying that you do so, or have done so.

2. What will you do if you refuse to close sincerely with God in Christ and do not accept his peace as it is offered? You have no other means of salvation; you must either do this or perish for ever. And if you do it with your heart, you may also say it with your tongue.

3. If people may be afraid to covenant with God because they will sin afterwards, then no one at all should covenant with God; for surely everyone will sin afterwards, if they live any length of time after the transaction. And we know of no way like this to keep people from falling. For if you covenant honestly with him, he undertakes, besides giving the new heart, to put his fear and law in it, and to give his Spirit to make you walk in his way. And when you covenant with God, you give yourself up to him to be sanctified and made to conform to his will. It is more a giving up of yourself to be led in his way in all things and kept from every evil way than any formal undertaking on your part to keep his way and avoid evil. So you need not be afraid of the covenant, whose language is, “Wilt thou not be made clean?” And all who avoid striking a covenant with God declare by it that they do not want to be made clean.

4. It is hard for anyone to say confidently that they will sin if such a temptation came in such and such circumstances, because people may think that God will either keep the temptation out of their way, or not let them be tempted beyond what they can bear, or give them a way of escape: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”—“There hath no temptation taken you, but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that you are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.” So the question is not what I may do afterwards, but what I now resolve to do. If my heart now charges me with any deceit or resolution to sin, I must lay that deceit aside before I covenant with God. But suppose my heart charges me with no such purpose; suppose I dare say that I resolve against every sin; and although I think I will fall before such and such a temptation, that thought does not come from any allowed and approved resolution to do so, but from knowing my own corruption and what I have done to provoke God to leave me; and the Lord knows that I do not resolve to sin, nor approve any secret inclination of my heart to such a sin, but would count it a special mercy to be kept from sin in such a case, and judge myself a wretched man because of the body of death within me that threatens to make me sin. In that case, I say, “my heart doth not condemn me, therefore I may and ought to have confidence before God.” If this is your case, I say to you: even if you should afterwards fail in many ways, and perhaps bring heavy temporal blows on yourself by it, and lose many signs of his love for a time, yet “there is an Advocate with the Father to plead thy pardon,” who has made satisfaction for our breaches: “He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way, and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” And for his sake God resolves to hold fast to the covenant with people after they sin: “If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments; if they break my statutes, and keep not my commandments;—Nevertheless, my loving-kindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail: my covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. Once have I sworn by my holiness.” Otherwise how could he be said “to betroth us unto himself for ever?” And how could the covenant be called “everlasting, ordered in all things and sure,” if there were no ground of comfort in it even when our house is not as it should be with God?

Indeed, it would be no better than the covenant of works if those who enter into it with God could depart from him again in such a way as to make it void for themselves and put themselves in a worse condition than they were in before they made it: “And I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from them to do them good”—compare Heb. 8:6: “But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much more also he is the Mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises.”—“The Lord hateth putting away.” No honest heart will stumble at this, but will rather be strengthened by it in duty: “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely; for mine anger is turned away from him.—Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them.” For other ties and bonds besides the fear of divorce and of punishment by death bind a noble-hearted wife to her duty; and so here people will “fear the Lord and his goodness.”

Objection. At the celebration of the Lord’s Supper, and on some other occasions, I have covenanted expressly and in words with God. But my fruitlessness in his ways, and my renewed suspicions about my state of grace, make me question whether I ever dealt with God sincerely; and I do not think I can do it any differently from the way I have done it.

Answer. 1. People are not to expect fruitfulness as great as they would like, nor full assurance of God’s favour, immediately after they have fled to Christ and dealt expressly with God in him. These things will keep a person busy all his days. The saints had their failings and shortcomings, and even backslidings, with many fits of dangerous unbelief, after they had very seriously, sincerely and expressly closed with God as their God in Christ.

2. Many look for fruitfulness in their lives, and for settledness of faith, from their own sincerity in dealing with God rather than from the Spirit of the Lord Jesus. They fix their hearts on their own honesty and resolutions, and not on the blessed root, Christ Jesus, without whom we can do nothing, and are altogether vanity even at our best. People should remember that one piece of grace cannot produce any degree of grace; nothing can work grace but the arm of Jehovah. If people would turn to Christ and covenant with him absolutely, as their duty, whatever may follow, looking to him alone for the fitting fruit, it would go better with them. God is not pleased when people turn to Christ and covenant with him for a while, to see whether such fruit and settledness will follow, intending to disown their interest in him and the covenant if such and such fruit does not appear within so much time. This is putting the ways of God to the test, and it greatly displeases him. People must close with Christ absolutely and covenant with him, resolving to stand by these things as their duty and as a ready way to bear fruit, whatever follows; having a testimony within them that they seriously aim at conforming to his revealed will in all things, and that they have entered into covenant with him for that end, as well as to be saved by it.

3. People should be slow to question their sincerity in dealing with God, unless they can prove the charge or have strong grounds for suspecting it. If you can find any deceit or guile in your dealing with him, you are bound to disown it and put it right, and to deal with God honestly and without guile. But suppose you know of no deceit or guile in yourself on the day you dealt with him. Suppose you can say that on that day you appealed to God that you were dealing honestly with him and did not intend to deceive, and begged him, according to his faithfulness, to search and test whether there was any crookedness in your way, and to show it to you and heal it—“Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts; and see if there be any wicked way in me; and lead me in the way everlasting”—and that afterwards you “came to the light, that your deeds might be manifest.” Suppose you can say that God’s answers to you from his word, as far as you could understand them, were answers of peace and confirmations of your sincerity. And further, suppose you dare say that if you had to deal with him again, on pain of life and death, you could do it no other way, nor intend more sincerity and seriousness than before. Then I dare say to you, in the Lord’s name, that you ought not to question your sincerity in dealing with God, but to “have confidence before God, since thy heart doth not condemn thee.” And you are bound to believe that “God dealeth uprightly with the upright man, and with the pure doth show himself pure.” If a person intends to be honest, God will not let him deceive himself; indeed, the Lord lets no one deceive himself unless he intends to deceive both God and people.

4. So put your unfruitfulness down to your lack of watchfulness and to your unbelief, and put your lack of full assurance down to an evil heart of unbelief, helped by Satan to work against the glorious free grace of God. Do not blame these things on a lack of sincerity in your closing with Christ. Resolve from now on to keep close to the root, and you will bear much fruit; and by much fruit you open yourselves to the witness of God’s Spirit, which will testify with your spirit that you have sincerely and honestly closed with God, and that the rest of your works are done in God and approved by him. So the witness of the Spirit and of the water joins with the blood, on which you are to lay the weight of your soul and conscience, and in which alone you are to sink the curses of the law due to you for all your sins and for your failings in your best things. These three agree in one: that this is the way of life and peace, and that you have an interest in it; and so you come to quietness and full assurance: “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine, no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit; for without me ye can do nothing.”—“He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me; and he that loveth me, shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him. If a man love me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.” “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.” “There are three that bear witness in earth, the spirit, and the water, and the blood; and these three agree in one.”

O blessed bargain of the new covenant, and thrice blessed Mediator of it! May he ride on in triumph, and subdue nations and languages, and gather in all his jewels: that honourable company of the firstborn, that stately troop of kings and priests, whose glory it will be to have washed their robes in the blood of that spotless Lamb, and whose happiness will flourish for ever in following him wherever he goes, and in being in the immediate company of the Ancient of Days, one sight of whose face will make them almost forget that they were ever on the earth. Oh, if only I could persuade people to believe that these things are not yes and no, and to hurry towards him who is hurrying to judge the world and to call people to account, especially for what they have made of this gospel! “Even so, come Lord Jesus!”

fields.title: The Whole Treatise in Questions and Answers
fields.body_html:
Question. WHAT is the great business a person has to do in the world?

Answer. To make sure of a saving interest in Christ Jesus, and to live in a way that fits it.

Q. 2. Do not all the members of the visible church have a saving interest in Christ?

A. No, indeed; only a very few of them have it.

Q. 3. How shall I know whether I have a saving interest in him?

A. Usually the Lord prepares his own way in the soul by a work of humbling. He shows a person his sin and misery, and so exercises him with it that he longs for the physician, Christ Jesus.

Q. 4. How shall I know whether I have been shown enough of my sin and misery?

A. A sufficient sight of it makes a person take salvation to heart above anything in this world. It makes him disown all relief in himself, even in his best things. It makes Christ, the Redeemer, very precious to the soul. It makes a person afraid to sin afterwards, and makes him content to be saved on whatever terms God pleases.

Q. 5. By what other ways may I discern a saving interest in him?

A. By my heart going out seriously and lovingly towards him as he is held out in the gospel; and this is faith, or believing.

Q. 6. How shall I know whether my heart goes out after him rightly, and whether my faith is true saving faith?

A. Where the heart goes out rightly after him in true and saving faith, the soul is pleased with Christ alone above all things, and is pleased with him in all his three offices, to rule and instruct as well as to save; and it is content to cleave to him, whatever hardships may follow.

Q. 7. What other mark of a saving interest in Christ can you give me?

A. Whoever is savingly in Christ is a new creature. He is graciously changed and renewed, in some measure, in his whole self and in all his ways, aiming at all the known commands of God.

Q. 8. What if I find sin getting the better of me now and then?

A. Although every sin deserves everlasting vengeance, yet if you are grieved for your failings, confess them to God with shame, resolve to strive against them honestly from now on, and flee to Christ for pardon, you will obtain mercy, and your interest stands sure.

Q. 9. What should someone do who cannot lay claim to Christ Jesus, nor to any of the marks spoken of?

A. Let him not rest until he has made sure of a saving interest in Christ for himself.

Q. 10. How can someone who has never had a saving interest in Christ until now make sure of one?

A. He must take to heart his sins and the great danger they put him in, and he must take to heart God’s offer of pardon and peace through Christ Jesus, and close wholeheartedly with God’s offer by turning to Christ, the blessed refuge.

Q. 11. What if my sins are unusually heinous, and great beyond the ordinary?

A. Whatever your sins are, if you will close with Christ Jesus by faith, you will never come into condemnation.

Q. 12. Is faith in Christ the only thing required of people?

A. Faith is the only condition on which God offers peace and pardon to people. But be sure of this: faith, if it is true and saving, will not be alone in the soul, but will be accompanied by true repentance and a thankful effort to conform to God’s image.

Q. 13. How shall I be sure that my heart accepts God’s offer and closes with Christ Jesus?

A. Go and make a covenant expressly, and say the thing to God in words.

Q. 14. How shall I do that?

A. Set apart some time, and, having considered your own lost state and the remedy offered by Christ Jesus, work your heart up to be pleased with that offer and to close with it. Then say to God expressly that you accept that offer, and accept him to be your God in Christ; that you give yourself up to him to be saved in his way, without reservation or exception in any case; and that from now on you will wait for salvation in the way he has appointed.

Q. 15. What if I break with God afterwards?

A. You must resolve in his strength not to break, keep watch over your own way, and put your heart in his hand for him to keep it. And if you break, you must confess it to God, judge yourself for it, flee to the Advocate for pardon, and resolve not to do it again; and you must do this as often as you fail.

Q. 16. How shall I come to full assurance of my interest in Christ, so that it is beyond dispute?

A. Learn to lay your weight on the blood of Christ, and aim at purity and holiness in every part of your conduct; and pray for the witness of God’s Spirit to join with the blood and the water. His testimony added to these will settle you in the faith of an interest in Christ.

Q. 17. What follows from closing with God in Christ in this way, by heart and mouth?

A. Union and communion with God, every good thing here, and his blessed fellowship in heaven for ever afterwards.

Q. 18. What if I make light of all these things, and do not take them to heart and put them into practice?

A. The Lord is coming with his angels in flaming fire to take vengeance on those who do not obey this gospel; and your judgment will be greater than the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all the greater because you have read this Treatise, for it will be a witness against you on that day.

FINIS.
